Jacob warns that driving his nursing flocks too hard for even one day would kill them (Genesis 33:13). The men of Gibeah pound on a door to drag out a guest and abuse him (Judges 19:22). In the Song of Solomon, the beloved knocks at the door…

h1853.sum: Diklah is one of the thirteen sons of Joktan named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:27). The Chronicler repeats his name in Israel's genealogical record (1 Chronicles 1:21). Through Joktan he descends from Shem by way of Arphaxad, Salah, and Eber. His name probably means "palm grove," a meaning drawn from a related Aramaic word for the date palm. Scripture records no deeds or words of his. Like his brothers, he…

h187.sum: Uzal was a son of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, and his name appears in the two parallel lists of nations in Genesis 10:27 and 1 Chronicles 1:21. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It is often associated with the idea of "going" or "departing," but the evidence does not settle the question. Like his brothers Sheba, Ophir, and Havilah, Uzal stands at the head of a people who settled toward southern…

h1877.sum: Desheʼ is the Hebrew word for fresh, young grass: the soft green growth that covers the ground after rain. The NKJV usually translates it "grass" or "herb," sometimes "tender grass," and once "green" in the familiar line "He makes me to lie down in green pastures" (Psalm 23:2). This tender growth depends on rain and light. When they come it springs up quickly, and when they are withheld it fails just as quickly.…

h1878.sum: The Hebrew verb dâshên means "to be fat" or "to make fat." In the ancient world, fatness meant richness, health, and the best portion of a thing. The same word can describe a prosperous life, a head soaked with fragrant oil, a sacrifice God receives with favor, and even the fat-soaked ashes cleared from the altar. The NKJV translates it many ways, including "accept," "anoint," "rich," "healthy," "prospered," "fat,"…

h188.sum: ʼôwy is a short Hebrew cry that names ruin and says whom it has reached. On some lips it is lament: Isaiah before the throne of God cries, "Woe is me, for I am undone!" On others it is panic, as when the Philistines learn that God has come into Israel's camp. From a prophet speaking for the Lord, it becomes a sentence of judgment: "Woe to the wicked!" Because the same cry can carry confession, terror, grief, or…

h1908.sum: Hadad is the name of at least three different Edomite men in the Old Testament. Two were early kings of Edom, listed among the rulers who reigned in the land of Esau's descendants before Israel had a king (Genesis 36:31–39; 1 Chronicles 1:43–51). The third, often called "Hadad the Edomite," is the one whose story Scripture actually tells. He was a royal child who escaped Joab's slaughter of Edom's men, grew up…

h1913.sum: Hadoram is the name of three different people in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused. The first is a son of Joktan, listed among Shem's descendants in the Table of Nations, whose family settled in Arabia (Genesis 10:27; 1 Chronicles 1:21). The second is a prince of Hamath, the son of King Tou, sent with gifts of gold, silver, and bronze to congratulate David on his victory over Hadadezer (1 Chronicles…

h1945.sum: Hôwy is the cry Israel raised over its dead, and the prophets carried that cry out of the graveyard and into the streets. Mourners said it beside a fresh tomb ("Alas, my brother!"). Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, Habakkuk, and others spoke it over people who were still alive and prospering. When a prophet cries "Woe" over the greedy, the drunken, or the self-serving shepherd, he is announcing God's judgment in the language…

h1950.sum: Homam was a Horite, a son of Lotan and a grandson of Seir, from the people who lived in the mountains of Seir before Esau's descendants took the land. His name appears only once in the Bible, in the Chronicler's genealogy (1 Chronicles 1:39). Genesis records the same man as Hemam (Genesis 36:22), a spelling difference that reflects a common interchange of two similar Hebrew letters. The meaning of the name is…

h1952.sum: The Hebrew word hôwn means a person's substance: the wealth, goods and possessions that make up what someone owns. The Bible uses it most in the wisdom books, especially Proverbs, where wise teachers weigh what wealth can and cannot do. Wealth can honor God. "Honor the LORD with your possessions" (Proverbs 3:9). It can also become a person's false fortress. The rich man's wealth is "like a high wall in his own…

h1961.g: am, became, become, becomes, been, being, belong, belonged, belonging, came, come, did, expressly, had, happen, happened, Has, has, have, Let, let, May, may, there, You, you
h1961.sum: The Hebrew verb hâyâh means "to be," "to become," or "to happen." English Bibles render it in many ways, including "was," "became," "it came to pass," and "it shall be." The common thread is reality taking hold. Something exists, something changes into a new condition, or something actually occurs in history. The word appears in God's first spoken command, "Let there be light" (Genesis 1:3). It carries the long…

h1980.g: away, brought, came, carry, cause, Come, come, coming, follow, followed, Go, go, goes, going, gone, had, has, lead, leads, led, made, Take, take, Walk, walk, walked, Walking, walking, Walks, walks, went
h1980.sum: Hâlak is the ordinary Hebrew verb for going and walking. It describes Abram setting out for Canaan, rivers flowing to the sea, messengers sent on errands, and armies marching to war. From that everyday movement, Scripture draws one of its most important pictures of human life. To "walk" is to live a certain way, in a certain direction, alongside someone or after something. The few words around the verb tell you…

h1992.sum: The Hebrew word hêm is the ordinary way of saying "they" when the group is masculine or mixed. It does more than stand in for a noun, though. Hebrew often builds a sentence with no verb for "is" or "are." In those sentences hêm names who or what is being described, and English translators supply the missing verb, as in "These are holy garments" (Leviticus 16:4). Hebrew verbs already show who is acting, so when a…

h1993.sum: The Hebrew verb hâmâh describes something stirred up and making noise: the sea crashing against the shore, a city in uproar, a crowd of enemies, dogs growling at night. The Bible also turns the same word inward. A troubled soul is "disquieted," a grieving heart wails "like flutes," and a loving heart "yearns." The word covers both the outward roar of a restless world and the inward churning of a person who is deeply…

h20.sum: The Hebrew word ʼăbaṭṭîyach means "melon," most likely the watermelon that grew well in Egypt's sandy soil along the Nile. It names an ordinary, refreshing fruit and carries no spiritual meaning of its own. It appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 11:5. There the Israelites, tired of the manna, weep as they remember the foods of Egypt: "the fish which we ate freely in Egypt, the cucumbers, the melons, the…

h2009.g: Behold, behold, Here, here, There, there
h2009.sum: Hinnêh is the Hebrew Bible's pointing word. With it a speaker says, in effect, "Look at this," and directs the listener's attention to a person, an event, or a fact that has just come into view. The narrator uses it to put the reader inside a character's moment of discovery: Jacob waking beside Leah, or Elisha's servant seeing a mountain full of fiery chariots. God uses it when He announces what He is about to do,…

h201.sum: Omar was a grandson of Esau, listed second among the sons of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn, and he became one of the clan chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 15; 1 Chronicles 1:36). The meaning of his name is probable but not certain. It most likely comes from the Hebrew verb ʼamar , "to say" or "to speak," and is often explained as "speaker" or "eloquent." Scripture tells us nothing about his words, deeds, or faith. He…

h2022.g: country, hill, hills, Mount, mount, mountain, Mountains, mountains, O
h2022.sum: The Hebrew word har is the Old Testament's ordinary word for a mountain. It can name a single peak such as Carmel or Hermon, a whole range of high country such as "the mountains of Ephraim," or a modest rise that English translators call a "hill." Because the NKJV renders the same word as "mountain" in some verses and "hill" in others, readers can miss a connection. The trembling "mountain" of Sinai and "the hill of…

h2029.sum: The Hebrew verb hârâh means "to conceive" or "to become pregnant." It names the hidden beginning of a life, the moment a child starts to exist before anyone can see it. Most of its uses appear in the family stories of Genesis and the historical books. There, the Bible records the conceptions of Isaac, Jacob and Esau, the sons of Leah and Rachel, Moses, Samuel, and others. Again and again the text places God at the…

h2042.sum: Hârâr is a Hebrew word for "mountain" or "hill." It is a fuller, more poetic form of the ordinary word for mountain. It appears mainly in psalms, blessings, and prophetic songs, where writers wanted the mountains to carry weight. Those are the oldest, heaviest, and most immovable things a person can see, and Scripture uses them to measure God. His righteousness "is like the great mountains" (Psalm 36:6). He owns…

h208.sum: Onam is the name of two different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused with each other or with Onan (H0209), the son of Judah whom the LORD put to death (Genesis 38). The first Onam was a Horite, a son of Shobal, from the people who lived in Mount Seir before Esau's descendants took the land (Genesis 36:23; 1 Chronicles 1:40). The second Onam belonged to the tribe of Judah. He was a son of…

h2091.sum: The Hebrew word zâhâb is the Old Testament's ordinary word for gold. It names the metal itself, the objects made from it, and the wealth it represents. Gold first appears in Eden, where Moses notes simply, "the gold of that land is good" (Genesis 2:12). From there it runs through the whole Old Testament: Egypt's riches carried out by Israel, the Tabernacle and Temple furnishings, kings' treasuries, idols, and the…

h211.sum: Ophir names both a man and a land in the Old Testament. The first is a man, a son of Joktan in the line of Shem, listed in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:29; 1 Chronicles 1:23). The second, and by far the more prominent, is a distant land so famous for its gold that "gold of Ophir" became Israel's way of naming the finest gold there was. Solomon's ships, built at Ezion Geber on the Red Sea and crewed alongside…

h2142.g: as, has, Make, recorder, Remember, remember, remembered, remembering, remembers, remembrance
h2142.sum: The Hebrew verb zâkar means "to remember." In Scripture, remembering is much more than recalling a fact. It means giving focused attention to a person, a promise or a past event in a way that leads to action. When God remembers Noah, the waters go down. When God remembers His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the Exodus begins. When Israel is told to remember the years in Egypt and the wilderness, the purpose…

h2158.sum: The Hebrew word zâmîyr means a song, especially a song of praise lifted to God. The NKJV renders it "songs," "psalms," "singing," and once "psalmist." It is a rare word, used only six times in the Old Testament. Those six uses cover nearly the whole range of life before God: a dying king, a sufferer in the dark, a traveler far from home, a congregation entering God's presence, a land waking up in spring, and a world…

h2175.sum: Zimran is a son of Abraham by Keturah. He is named first among her six sons in Genesis 25:2 and again in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 1:32. Those two verses are the only places Scripture mentions him, and neither records anything he said or did. The meaning of his name is uncertain. It most likely comes from the Hebrew root zamar , which can mean "to sing" or "make music," suggesting something like "musician" or…

h2190.sum: Zaavan was a Horite, a son of Ezer and a grandson of Seir the Horite. His family lived in Mount Seir before the descendants of Esau took the land. His name probably means "trembling" or "disquieted," from a Hebrew root meaning to tremble or be agitated, though the derivation is not certain. Scripture names him only twice, in the matching genealogies of Genesis 36:27 and 1 Chronicles 1:42, and records nothing he said…

h2220.g: arm, arms, force, forces, O, own, strength
h2220.sum: The Hebrew word zᵉrôwaʻ means "arm." It names the actual limb of a person, or the shoulder cut of a sacrificed animal. In the Old Testament, though, the arm most often stands for strength put into action, the power to fight, rescue, build, carry, or rule. Some English translations render it "strength," "power," "authority," or even military "forces." When Scripture speaks of the LORD's arm, it means God acting in…

h2226.sum: Zerah is a Hebrew name shared by several different men in the Old Testament. It comes from a verb meaning "to rise," "to shine," or "to appear," the word used for the sun coming up, so the name means something like "rising" or "dawning." The best known is Zerah the son of Judah and Tamar. He was the twin whose hand came out first at birth and received the midwife's scarlet thread, only for his brother Perez to break…

h2254.g: acted, as, broken, destroy, hold, pledge, take, taken, you
h2254.sum: The Hebrew word châbal covers a surprising range: taking a pledge for a loan, acting corruptly or bringing ruin, and writhing in labor to bring forth a child. A closely related noun, which older numbering lists with this word, gives a shepherd's staff its name, "Bonds." Behind several of these uses lies the picture of something wound or drawn tight. A creditor binds a borrower with collateral. Ruin twists a thing…

h2261.sum: The Hebrew word chăbatstseleth names a wildflower that the NKJV, following long English tradition, translates "rose." Scripture uses it only twice. Most students of the land of Israel think it was a spring meadow flower that grows from a bulb, such as a crocus, narcissus, or asphodel. It was not the cultivated garden rose of later centuries. It was the kind of flower that covers an open field after the rains, lovely…

h2263.g: Embrace, embrace, embraced, embraces, embracing, folds
h2263.sum: The Hebrew verb châbaq means "to embrace": to wrap one's arms around someone or something and hold on. Most often it describes a real embrace. Laban greets his nephew Jacob, Esau receives the brother who cheated him, and an old, nearly blind Jacob holds the grandsons he never expected to see. Elisha uses the word for a promise to a childless woman: "you shall embrace a son." In the Song of Solomon, the bride rests…

h2270.sum: The Hebrew word châbêr means a companion, associate, or fellow: someone joined to others by a shared cause, a shared life, or a shared loyalty. It can describe tribes standing together, a friend who lifts you when you fall, or the friends of a bridegroom. The word itself carries no moral value. Scripture speaks of the companions of thieves as readily as the companions of those who fear God. Across its uses, however,…

h2288.sum: The Hebrew word chăgâv means a cleft or crevice in a rock: a narrow, hidden opening high in a cliff where a bird can nest or a people can shelter out of reach. Scripture uses it only three times, and each time the NKJV renders it "the clefts of the rock." Because the word is so rare, each use carries weight, and the three uses form a striking contrast.

h2301.sum: Hadad was the eighth listed of the twelve sons of Ishmael, which made him a grandson of Abraham through Hagar. Under this Strong's entry his name appears only once, in the Chronicler's list of Ishmael's sons (1 Chronicles 1:30). The parallel list in Genesis 25:15 names the same son "Hadar," a difference usually explained by the close resemblance of two Hebrew letters. His name comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be…

h2315.sum: Cheder is the Hebrew word for the inner room of a house: the bedroom, the private chamber, the room farthest from the street. Joseph went there to weep when he could no longer hold back his tears. A defeated king ran there to hide, and a bride rejoiced that "the king has brought me into his chambers." Because it was the most private place a person had, the word carries ideas of intimacy, secrecy, refuge, and danger.…

h2319.sum: The Hebrew word châdâsh means "new" or "fresh." It can describe something just made or never used, such as a new cart, new ropes, or a new house. It can also describe someone newly arrived, or something God does that has never been done before. In ordinary life it marks the difference between the untried and the worn. In the hands of the psalmists and prophets it becomes one of Scripture's great words of hope: a new…

h2336.g: hook, hooks, thickets, thistle, thistles, thorn, Thorns, thorns
h2336.sum: The Hebrew word chôwach names a thistle, thorn, or bramble, the prickly wild growth that takes over where nothing good is planted. In two passages the same word names a hook, the sharp tool used to seize a powerful creature by the jaw or to lead away a captive.

h2339.sum: The Hebrew word chûwṭ means a thread or cord. It is a thin, spun fiber, and the NKJV translates it "thread," "cord," "line," or "strand." The word appears only seven times in the Old Testament, yet those few uses carry real weight. A single thread can stand for the smallest possible amount of anything, as when Abram refuses even "a thread" from the king of Sodom. A thread can picture weakness, as when Samson snaps…

h2340.sum: "Hivite" is the name of one of the peoples living in Canaan before and during Israel's entry into the land. The word means nothing beyond the name of this people. Its importance comes from the role the Hivites play in God's dealings with Israel. Usually they appear in the familiar lists of nations God promised to drive out, and those lists repeatedly remind Israel that the land would be received by the Lord's power,…

h2341.sum: Havilah is a name the Bible uses for more than one thing. It first appears as a land in the opening chapters of Genesis, a territory encircled by the Pishon, one of the four rivers that flowed out of Eden, and Moses pauses to say that its gold "is good" and that bdellium and onyx are found there (Genesis 2:11–12). Later, the Table of Nations gives the name to two different men, a son of Cush in Ham's line (Genesis…

h2343.sum: Hul was a son of Aram and a grandson of Shem. He belongs to the generations after the Flood, listed in the Table of Nations in Genesis 10. Scripture names him only twice, in Genesis 10:23 and again in the Chronicler's genealogy at 1 Chronicles 1:17. No story is told about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. It has been tentatively linked to the idea of a "circle" or to the Hebrew word for "sand," but neither…

h2346.g: O, two, Wall, wall, walled, walls
h2346.sum: The Hebrew word chôwmâh means "wall," most often the massive stone wall that surrounded an ancient city. A wall separated a secure city from an open village, kept enemies out, gave defenders a place to stand and watch, and gave the people inside a sense of identity and permanence. For that reason the Old Testament's story of walls is also a story about where people place their trust. Jericho's wall fell flat at a…

h2351.sum: The Hebrew word chûwts means outside . It names whatever lies beyond a boundary: outside a tent, a house, a veil, a city wall, or the camp of Israel. Because the outside of a town is its open public space, the word is often translated "street" or "streets." Occasionally it means "fields," the open country beyond settled land. The word itself is plain and physical. Its weight comes from what stands on the inside and…

h2356.sum: The Hebrew word chôwr means a hole: a hollow or opening in something solid. The word occurs 7 times in 7 verses of the Hebrew Bible, and in each place the setting tells you what kind of hole it is. It can be a cave in the earth, a hole bored in a wooden lid, a breach in a wall, the opening in a door, or the hollow where an eye sits in the skull. The word itself is simple. What makes it worth studying is what happens…

h2367.sum: Husham was one of the early kings of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. Scripture says only that he came "of the land of the Temanites," that he followed Jobab of Bozrah on the throne, and that Hadad the son of Bedad succeeded him when he died (Genesis 36:34–35; 1 Chronicles 1:45–46). His name is traditionally understood to mean "haste" or "hasty," from a Hebrew root meaning to hurry, though the Bible never…

h2368.sum: The Hebrew word chôwthâm means a signet or seal. A signet was a small engraved stone or metal object, worn as a ring or on a cord around the neck. Its owner pressed it into soft clay or wax to leave his own distinctive mark. Because the impression was a distinctive, recognized mark of that one carving, the signet stood for the person himself. It proved who he was, guaranteed his word, and carried his authority. When…

h2372.g: look, saw, See, see, seeing, seen, sees
h2372.sum: The Hebrew verb châzâh means to see, look at, or behold. Most often it describes careful, attentive seeing: watching something closely enough to understand it. Scripture uses it for ordinary observation, such as noticing a skilled worker or looking over a neglected field. It is also the word for what the prophets "saw" when the Lord gave them His message, and for the false visions of prophets who spoke from their…

h2406.sum: The Hebrew word chiṭṭâh means wheat , the most valued grain of ancient Israel. Scripture uses it for the growing crop, the threshed grain, and the flour baked into bread. Because wheat was the best of Israel's daily food, it became a natural measure of God's care. He promised to feed a listening people with "the finest of wheat" (Psalm 81:16). He required wheat flour for the bread that consecrated Israel's priests,…

h2416.g: alive, animal, Life, life, live, lived, lives, Living, living, raw
h2416.sum: The Hebrew word chay means "living" or "alive." It is one of the Old Testament's most common ways of speaking about life. It describes animals and wild beasts, a person's lifetime, fresh flowing water, and even raw, exposed flesh. Above all, it describes God Himself as "the living God," the One by whose life Israel swore its most solemn oaths. The same word that names the tree of life in Eden also names the fierce…

h2441.sum: The Hebrew word chêk names the palate, the roof and inner part of the mouth where food is tasted and words are formed. The NKJV usually translates it "mouth," sometimes "taste," and once "palate." Biblical writers take this small, ordinary part of the body and use it to describe what goes on inside a person: what we test, what we enjoy, what we keep, and what we say. Job asks, "Cannot my taste discern the unsavory?"…

h2461.sum: The Hebrew word châlâb means "milk," the everyday milk of goats, sheep, and cows that sustained families in ancient Israel. It was ordinary food. Proverbs promises "enough goats' milk for your food" (Proverbs 27:27). It was also the food of honored hospitality, as when Abraham set milk before the three visitors who came when the LORD appeared to him (Genesis 18:8). Because milk meant healthy flocks, good pasture,…

h2470.g: became, entreat, entreated, grieved, has, severe, sick, themselves, weak, wounded
h2470.sum: The Hebrew verb châlâh most often means to be sick, weak, wounded, or worn down. It describes kings on their deathbeds, a soldier struck by an arrow, Samson drained of strength, a heart sick with grief, and a bride sick with love. The prophets use it for the "severe" wound of a nation that has turned from God, a wound no human remedy can treat. The same verb also has a second use: to entreat someone's favor, to…

h2474.sum: The Hebrew word challôwn means a window: an opening in the wall of a house, palace, city wall, ark, or temple. Ancient windows had no glass. They were open gaps, often covered with wooden lattice, that let in light and air and allowed people inside to watch the world outside. Because a window breaks through a protective wall, Scripture repeatedly places important moments at this boundary between inside and outside,…

h2481.sum: The Hebrew word chălîy names a crafted piece of jewelry: an ornament that a skilled worker shaped from precious material. It appears only twice in the Old Testament, both times in poetry and both times as a picture of something precious. In Proverbs 25:12, a wise rebuke received by a listening ear is "like an earring of gold and an ornament of fine gold." In Song of Solomon 7:1, the bridegroom says the curves of his…

h2498.g: change, changed, pass, passed, passes, pierced, renew, sprout, up
h2498.sum: The Hebrew verb châlaph describes movement from one state to another. Something passes by, sweeps through, pierces through, is exchanged for something else, or springs up fresh. English versions translate it with words as varied as "changed," "substitute," "pass," "sprout," "renew," and "abolish." The word itself is neutral. It can describe Jacob's household putting on clean garments before worship, Laban cheating…

h251.sum: The Hebrew word ʼâch means "brother." Its starting point is a male sibling, such as Cain and Abel or Joseph and his brothers. Scripture widens it to cover a nephew, a clansman, a fellow Israelite, or a fellow Levite serving at the house of God. In a common idiom, "a man to his brother," it simply means "one another." The NKJV renders it most often as "brother," "brothers," and "brethren."

h2526.sum: Ham was one of the three sons of Noah, a man who lived through the flood inside the ark and stepped out into a washed world under God's blessing. His name is usually connected with a Hebrew root meaning "warm" or "hot." That link is common but not certain, and a proposed connection with an Egyptian word for Egypt as the "black land" remains unproven. Scripture gives us only one scene from Ham's own life. After the…

h2530.g: covet, delight, desirable, desire, desired, desires, precious
h2530.sum: The Hebrew verb châmad describes a strong inward attraction, the pull of the heart toward something it finds beautiful, valuable, or pleasing. English translations render it "covet," "desire," "delight," "pleasant," or "desirable," and each choice depends on what the heart is reaching for. In Eden God Himself made trees "pleasant to the sight" (Genesis 2:9). David says God's judgments are "more to be desired… than…

h2535.sum: The Hebrew word chammâh means "heat," and in the Old Testament's poetry it becomes a name for the sun, the sun as people feel it. It does not simply point to a light in the sky. It describes the sun's burning warmth, its dazzling brightness and its reach into every corner of the earth. The word appears only six times, all in poetry and prophecy. The NKJV renders it "heat" once and "sun" five times.

h2542.sum: The Hebrew word chammûwq means a curve or rounded contour of the body. The NKJV translates it "curves," and older translations such as the KJV render it "joints." It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:1, where the bridegroom praises his bride: "The curves of your thighs are like jewels, The work of the hands of a skillful workman." Because the word is used only once, everything we know about its…

h2559.sum: The Hebrew verb châmaq means to turn away or slip off, and in one of its uses it means turning this way and that. It appears only twice in the Old Testament, and both times it describes what goes wrong between two people who love each other. In the Song of Solomon the bride finally opens the door, only to find that "my beloved had turned away and was gone" (Song 5:6). In Jeremiah the Lord asks His unfaithful people,…

h2566.sum: Hamran is a Horite, a member of the people who lived in the hill country of Seir before Esau's descendants took it over. He appears only once under this spelling, in 1 Chronicles 1:41, where he is the first-named son of Dishon. The parallel list in Genesis 36:26 calls the same man Hemdan, a separately indexed name (H2533). The meaning of Hamran is probable rather than certain. It likely comes from a Hebrew root…

h2577.sum: "Hamathite" is the name of one of the families descended from Canaan, the grandson of Noah through Ham. The word appears only twice in Scripture, both times in genealogies. Genesis 10:18 lists the Hamathite last among Canaan's sons, and 1 Chronicles 1:16 repeats the same list centuries later. The name comes from Hamath, a city on the Orontes River in what is now Syria. A Hamathite is someone who belongs to the…

h2585.sum: The Hebrew name Chănôwk belongs to four men and one city. English Bibles usually spell it "Enoch" in Genesis 4–5 and "Hanoch" elsewhere. The best known is Enoch the son of Jared, the seventh generation from Adam through Seth, the father of Methuselah, and the great-grandfather of Noah. The name is generally connected to the Hebrew verb ḥānak , "to train, dedicate, or inaugurate," so it most likely means "dedicated"…

h259.sum: ʼEchâd is the ordinary Hebrew word for "one." It counts things: one cubit, one ram, one silver platter. It also marks the first day of a month, singles out "each" curtain or "a certain" man, and pairs "one" with "the other." The NKJV renders it many ways, including "first," "each," "another," "once," "alone," and "same." Most of its uses are plain counting, and many cluster in the detailed instructions for Israel's…

h2590.sum: The Hebrew verb chânaṭ is a rare word that describes two very different processes. It is usually connected with spices and aroma. In Genesis 50 it describes embalming, the careful treatment of a dead body so that it would not decay. In the Song of Solomon it describes the fig tree as it "puts forth her green figs" when spring arrives. The word is rare: it occurs 5 times in 4 verses of the Hebrew Bible (Genesis 50:2…

h2637.sum: Châçêr is the Hebrew verb for lacking, falling short, or running low. It can describe floodwaters going down, a number coming up short, a jar of oil running dry, or a person going without bread. It names the gap between what is needed and what is on hand. Scripture uses this ordinary word to make some of its most comforting promises: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1).

h2654.g: delight, delighted, delights, desire, desired, does, pleased, pleases, pleasure
h2654.sum: The Hebrew verb châphêts describes a heart that leans toward something. It means to delight in, to desire, to be pleased with, or simply to want. The word can be ordinary. In Deuteronomy 25:7 it describes a man who does not want to marry his brother's widow. It can also express strong personal desire, as when Shechem delights in Jacob's daughter (Genesis 34:19). Its greatest weight in Scripture comes from how often…

h2660.sum: Hepher is a Hebrew name that most likely means "pit" or "well." It comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to search out." The Old Testament uses it for several unrelated people and places, and they should not be merged. The most important is Hepher the Manassite, a son of Gilead and the father of Zelophehad. When Zelophehad died in the wilderness with five daughters and no sons, his family line seemed headed for…

h269.sum: The Hebrew word ʼâchôwth means "sister." Most often it names an actual female sibling, such as Miriam watching over baby Moses, Rachel envying Leah, Dinah avenged by her brothers, or Tamar wronged by her half-brother Amnon. Hebrew also uses the word in an everyday phrase, literally "a woman to her sister," to say that things are joined "one to another." Scripture uses this phrase for the coupled curtains of the…

h2700.sum: Hazarmaveth is a son of Joktan and a great-great-great-grandson of Shem. He appears only twice in Scripture, both times in the list of Noah's descendants known as the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20). His name joins two Hebrew words, chatsar , "court," "village," or "settlement," and maveth , "death," so it means "Court of Death" or "Village of Death." Scripture never explains why anyone would…

h2737.sum: The Hebrew word chârûwz means a string of beads or jewels worn around the neck. Scripture uses it only once, in Song of Solomon 1:10. There the bridegroom king looks at his bride and says, "Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments, Your neck with chains." The word names a real piece of jewelry: small precious pieces threaded together into one necklace.

h275.sum: Ahuzzam was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 4:6. He was a son of Ashhur, "the father of Tekoa," and Ashhur's wife Naarah, and his name heads the list of her four sons. His name comes from the Hebrew verb meaning "to grasp" or "to take possession," and it probably means "possessor" or "their possession." The exact sense is uncertain. Scripture tells us nothing about his…

h2753.sum: Hori is a Hebrew proper name connected with the ancient Horites, the people who lived in the rugged hill country of Mount Seir, south of the Dead Sea, before Esau's descendants took the land. Under this one Strong's entry stand three distinct realities: Hori the son of Lotan, a grandson of "Seir the Horite" (Genesis 36:22; 1 Chronicles 1:39); the Horite people and their chiefs as a group (Genesis 36:20, 30;…

h2762.sum: The Hebrew word cherek means "lattice." It describes the crisscrossed grille set into a window opening in an ancient house. A lattice let in air and light and allowed people to see through it, yet it still kept a boundary between inside and outside. The word appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 2:9. There the beloved runs across the hills to the young woman's home and stands outside it: "Behold, he…

h2768.sum: Hermon is the great snow-capped mountain at the far northern edge of the land God gave Israel. It rises more than nine thousand feet at the southern end of the Anti-Lebanon range and towers over everything around it. Its name most likely comes from a Hebrew root meaning to set apart or to devote , so Hermon probably means something like sacred or set-apart mountain . That meaning is probable rather than certain. It…

h28.sum: Abida was a grandson of Abraham through Midian, one of the six sons Abraham had with Keturah. He appears only twice in Scripture, both times in a list: "the sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abidah, and Eldaah" (Genesis 25:4; 1 Chronicles 1:33). The NKJV spells his name "Abidah" in Genesis and "Abida" in Chronicles, but the Hebrew name is the same. It is built from the words for "father" and "to know," and…

h2809.sum: Heshbon was a city on the high plateau east of the Jordan River. When Israel came out of the wilderness, it was the royal city of Sihon, king of the Amorites. The name probably means "reckoning" or "device." It comes from a Hebrew root that means to think, plan, or calculate. Heshbon appears nearly forty times from Numbers to Jeremiah. It earlier belonged to Moab, then became Sihon's capital, and was captured by…

h2845.sum: Heth is named in the Bible's family table of nations as a son of Canaan, listed right after Canaan's firstborn, Sidon (Genesis 10:15; 1 Chronicles 1:13). His name lives on mainly through his descendants, "the sons of Heth" and "the daughters of Heth," a Canaanite community living around Hebron in the days of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The name is often connected with a Hebrew root meaning "to be shattered" or "to be…

h2856.g: Seal, seal, Sealed, sealed, seals, up
h2856.w: Seal, Seal Up, Make An End
h2856.sum: The Hebrew verb châtham means to seal , to press a mark of authority onto something or to close it off so it stays secure. In Esther, a decree sealed with the king's ring could not be revoked. Jeremiah sealed a deed to a field. Prophets sealed visions until God's time to open them. The same verb can also mean simply to stop up or shut , as when a flow is stopped or stars are hidden from sight.

h2861.sum: The Hebrew word chăthunnâh means "wedding," the day a marriage is celebrated. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 3:11. There the daughters of Zion are called to come out and see King Solomon wearing the crown his mother placed on him "on the day of his wedding, the day of the gladness of his heart." In this single use, Scripture defines the wedding day as the king's day of joy. The wedding…

h2895.w: Be Pleasing, Go Well, Do Good
h2895.sum: The Hebrew verb ṭôwb means to be good in action or effect: to be pleasing, to go well, or to do good to someone. It describes goodness in motion. A plan seems good to a king, life goes well for a people, a heart is refreshed, or God sets Himself to bless. English translations render it in many ways, including "well," "pleases," "good," "better," "lovely," and even "embellished."

h2896.g: better, fine, Good, good, goodness, goods, kind, pleasant
h2896.sum: Ṭôwb is the Old Testament's ordinary word for "good." It covers a wide range: a ripe fig, a handsome young man, a merry heart, a fertile land, wise advice, a righteous life, and the character of God Himself. At its heart the word describes something that is as it ought to be, whether useful, pleasing, beneficial, or right. Context decides which of these is meant. The same word that calls Rebekah "very beautiful to…

h2918.sum: The Hebrew word ṭîyrâh names an enclosure: a ring of stones or tents around a camp, a settlement where a clan kept its flocks, or a course of masonry built around or on top of something. The NKJV translates it as "settlements," "encampments," "forts," "dwelling place," "battlement," and "rows." The word is rare. It occurs only seven times in seven verses of the Hebrew Bible, but those seven uses cover a wide range…

h2919.sum: The Hebrew word ṭal means dew , the moisture that settles on grass, fields and fleece during the night. In Israel's long, rainless summers, dew was a source of moisture during the dry months that could benefit plants. For that reason Scripture treats it as more than a pleasant feature of the morning. When Isaac blesses Jacob, his first request is "the dew of heaven" (Genesis 27:28). When the returned exiles leave…

h2936.sum: The Hebrew word ṭânaph means "to soil" or "to get dirty." It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 5:3, where the NKJV translates it "defile." It describes ordinary physical dirt, the kind feet pick up when they touch the ground. It does not describe sin, religious uncleanness, or moral corruption. The bride in the Song has gone to bed. Her beloved knocks at the door, and she answers with an excuse: "I…

h2983.sum: The Hebrew word translated "Jebusite" names a Canaanite people who lived in the central hill country and held the city of Jebus, later known as Jerusalem. It is a people name and carries no hidden meaning. The Jebusites first appear in the table of nations, then in God's repeated lists of peoples whose land He promised to Abraham and his descendants. Long after Israel entered Canaan, they still held Jerusalem. Judah…

h3.sum: The Hebrew word ʼêb means freshness or fresh green growth: the shoots and greenery of living plants. The word occurs 2 times in 2 verses of the Hebrew Bible, both in poetry. Because the word is so rare, the two verses speak with special force when read side by side. In Job 8:12, a papyrus plant stands green and uncut in the marsh, yet "it withers before any other plant." In Song of Solomon 6:11, someone goes down to…

h3027.g: both, hand, handed, Hands, hands, Monument, monument, own, power, side, times
h3027.sum: The Hebrew word yâd means hand . It can be the hand that holds a staff, wears a bracelet, or grips a sword. Because the hand is how a person acts, Hebrew also used yâd for what a person can do and what a person controls: power, authority, custody, and agency. To fall "into the hand" of an enemy is to come under his control. A word spoken "by the hand of" a prophet is God's word carried through a human messenger.…

h3045.g: acknowledge, acquaintance, acquaintances, acquainted, become, certainly, consider, directed, has, instructed, knew, Know, know, knowing, known, knows, made, Make, make, making, perceive, perceived, show, taught, teach, You, you
h3045.sum: The Hebrew verb yâdaʻ means to know , and the setting decides what kind of knowing is meant. A person can know a fact, and can also know another person, know how to do something with skilled hands, or be known by God with chosen and caring attention. The same word describes Adam knowing Eve, Pharaoh's officials realizing Egypt was ruined, craftsmen who knew how to build the tabernacle, and God telling Israel, "You…

h3050.sum: Yâhh (Yah) is a short, poetic form of God's personal name, Yahweh, the name God revealed to Israel as the One who rescues and stays with His people. In most English Bibles it is hidden behind the capitalized word "LORD." The NKJV prints "YAH" in a few places, such as Psalm 68:4, Isaiah 12:2, Isaiah 26:4, and Isaiah 38:11. The shortened name appears mainly in songs and prayers. It first appears in Israel's song at…

h310.sum: The Hebrew word ʼachar means "behind" or "after." In its simplest use it tells where someone stands, at the rear of another, or when something happens: "after these things," "afterward." Scripture uses it hundreds of times to move its stories forward, from the genealogies of Genesis to the reigns of the kings. Because the Bible so often pictures life as a walk, "behind" naturally comes to mean following. To walk…

h3103.sum: Jobab is a Hebrew name shared by at least five different men in the Old Testament. One is a son of Joktan in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:29). Another is an early king of Edom from the city of Bozrah (Genesis 36:33–34). A third is the king of Madon who joined Jabin of Hazor against Joshua (Joshua 11:1). The last two are Benjamites named in the Chronicler's family records (1 Chronicles 8:9, 18). The meaning of…

h3117.g: always, daily, Day, day, Days, days, day’s, this, today, today’s, two, year, years
h3117.sum: The Hebrew word yôwm means "day." It can name a full day, evening and morning together, the hours of daylight, or "today." It can also stretch to cover a lifetime ("all the days of my life"), an era ("in the days of the judges"), or a habit ("day by day"). Context decides which one is meant, and the Old Testament uses the word in every one of its books.

h3120.sum: Javan is first a man and then a people. Genesis names him as the fourth-listed son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah. His descendants spread through the "coastlands," the islands and shores of the Mediterranean, and in later Scripture his name stands for the Greek world. The name is the Hebrew equivalent of the Greek word for the Ionians, the Greeks of the Aegean coast and islands who were the first Greeks most Near…

h3123.sum: The Hebrew word yôwnâh simply means dove or pigeon . It names the gentle, ordinary bird that Israelites saw nesting in rock cliffs, heard cooing in the valleys, and brought to the tabernacle when they could not afford a lamb. Scripture draws on what everyone knew about doves: their soft mourning call, their quick and nervous flight, their habit of hiding in clefts of rock, and their instinct to fly home.

h3126.sum: The Hebrew word yôwnêq means "one who nurses," a suckling infant still drawing life from its mother. Hebrew also used the word for a young shoot that springs up from a plant's roots and lives off that root system, much as an infant lives at the breast. In both uses the word pictures something small and alive that cannot yet live on its own.

h3195.sum: Jetur was a son of Ishmael and a grandson of Abraham through Hagar. He is listed tenth among Ishmael's twelve sons (Genesis 25:15; 1 Chronicles 1:31), and his name later identifies a people descended from him who lived east of the Jordan. The name probably means "enclosure" or "encampment," perhaps the circular camp of a herding people, though the derivation is not certain. Scripture records no words or deeds of…

h3201.g: able, endure, prevail, prevailed, prevailing, you
h3201.sum: The Hebrew word yâkôl means to be able . It measures what a person can or cannot do, bear, or overcome. In the NKJV it appears as "can," "could," "able," "prevail," "endure," and sometimes "may" or "must." The word is ordinary. It describes a land too small for two herds, eyes too dim to see, and a riddle no one could solve. Scripture also uses it at the decisive edges of life with God, where human strength runs out.

h3205.g: ancestry, bear, bearing, bears, beget, begets, begot, begotten, birth, bore, born, borne, bring, brings, cause, child, children, fathered, gave, give, given, have, midwife, midwives
h3205.sum: Yâlad is the ordinary Hebrew verb for bringing new life into the world. A mother bears a child, a father begets a son, a child is born, and a midwife helps bring the baby out. Because every family line runs through birth, this is the word that drives the genealogies of Genesis and Chronicles. Its long chains of "begot" record how God kept His promise alive from Adam to David, generation after generation of people…

h3212.g: away, brought, came, carry, cause, Come, come, coming, follow, followed, Go, go, goes, going, gone, had, has, lead, leads, led, made, Take, take, Walk, walk, walked, Walking, walking, Walks, walks, went
h3212.sum: The Hebrew verb yâlak is one of the Old Testament's everyday words for movement. It means to walk, go, come, or depart. It describes Abram leaving Haran, armies on the march, a daughter-in-law setting out for Bethlehem, and a prophet carrying a linen sash to the Euphrates. Because Scripture pictures a human life as a road, the same word also describes how a person lives. People "walk" in God's ways, or they "walk…

h3225.sum: The Hebrew word yâmîyn means right , as in the right hand, the right side, or the direction to one's right. For someone facing east toward the sunrise, the right also pointed south, so the same word can name a direction. Because most people do their strongest and most skillful work with the right hand, the word naturally came to stand for strength, favor, and honor. Jacob blesses with his right hand. A king seats an…

h3245.g: appointed, founded, founding, had, Have, themselves, You
h3245.w: Found, Lay A Foundation, Establish, Appoint
h3245.sum: The Hebrew verb yâçad means to found something: to lay a foundation, to establish, or to appoint. Builders use it for the costly stones beneath Solomon's temple and for the foundation laid when the exiles returned to rebuild the temple. Poets and prophets use it for God laying the foundations of the earth, a picture of His authority over everything that stands on it. The same verb describes appointing people to an…

h3266.sum: Jeush is the name of four different men in the Bible, and they should not be confused with one another. The first is an Edomite chief, a son of Esau by his wife Aholibamah (Genesis 36:18; 1 Chronicles 1:35). The second is a Gershonite Levite, a son of Shimei, listed in David's organization of the Levites (1 Chronicles 23:10–11). The third is a Benjaminite from King Saul's family line through Jonathan (1 Chronicles…

h3281.sum: Jaalam was a son of Esau by his wife Aholibamah. He was born in the land of Canaan and later became a clan chief among Esau's descendants in Edom (Genesis 36:5, 14, 18; 1 Chronicles 1:35). His name probably means "concealed" or "hidden." It comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to hide," though the derivation is not absolutely certain. Scripture says nothing of his deeds, words, or faith. What it preserves is his place…

h3292.sum: Jaakan was a son of the Horite chief Ezer and a descendant of Seir the Horite. These were the people who lived in the hill country of Seir before Esau's descendants took it over. Scripture names him only once under this spelling, in the Chronicler's list of Seir's family: "The sons of Ezer were Bilhan, Zaavan, and Jaakan" (1 Chronicles 1:42). The parallel list in Genesis 36:27 names the same man as Akan, a…

h3293.sum: The Hebrew word yaʻar means a forest, woods, or thicket. It describes the dense, uncultivated land beyond the farmer's fields and the city walls, where trees grow thick, paths disappear, and lions and bears make their home. The same Hebrew spelling, indexed under the same Strong's number, also includes the word the NKJV translates "honeycomb" in Song of Solomon 5:1. Scripture uses yaʻar for real places, such as the…

h3302.sum: The Hebrew verb yâphâh means to be beautiful or to be fair , and in some settings to make beautiful or to decorate . Scripture uses it only eight times, and each use carries weight. It describes the King of Psalm 45, who is "fairer than the sons of men." It voices a bridegroom's delight in his bride in the Song of Solomon. It also appears in the prophets, where Ezekiel shows the Lord turning an abandoned infant into…

h3303.sum: The Hebrew word yâpheh means "beautiful," "fair," "lovely," or "fine." Most often it describes how someone or something looks: Sarah and Rachel, Joseph and David, Absalom and Esther, even the sleek cows in Pharaoh's dream. Scripture never treats this kind of beauty as goodness. Again and again a beautiful person becomes the center of danger, desire, or deception. Absalom had no blemish "from the sole of his foot to…

h3315.sum: Japheth was one of the three sons of Noah, a brother of Shem and Ham, who entered the ark with his wife and survived the flood. His name is connected to the Hebrew idea of being open, wide, or spacious, so it is commonly understood as "enlarged" or "he will enlarge." Genesis itself makes the link through wordplay when Noah prays, "May God enlarge Japheth" (Genesis 9:27). His name appears only eleven times, all in…

h3318.g: Bring, bring, bringing, brings, brought, came, Come, come, comes, coming, continuously, forth, forward, Go, go, goes, going, gone, has, issued, lead, led, out, projecting, projects, put, send, spreads, take, took, went
h3318.sum: Yâtsâʼ is one of the Old Testament's everyday verbs of movement. It means to go out or come out of a place, and in its causative use it means to bring someone or something out. People go out of tents, cities, and countries. Armies go out to battle. Slaves go out free. Children come from their parents' bodies, plants come up from the ground, water flows from a source, and words come out of a mouth. The word points to…

h3327.sum: Isaac was the son God promised to Abraham and Sarah long after they were too old to have children. He married Rebekah, became the father of Esau and Jacob, and is the middle name in the title God gave Himself: "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." His name means "he laughs" or "laughter," from the Hebrew verb for laughing. Genesis builds his story around that word. Abraham fell on his face and laughed at the…

h3336.sum: The Hebrew word yêtser means "something formed." Sometimes it refers to a physical thing that has been shaped, such as a clay pot, a carved idol, or the human body made from dust. More often it refers to what the heart forms inwardly: the settled bent of a person's thoughts, purposes and desires. The NKJV translates it as "intent," "imagination," "inclination," "mind," "frame," "formed," and "mold." It appears only…

h3355.sum: Joktan was a son of Eber and a descendant of Shem who lived in the generations after the flood. Genesis introduces him beside his brother Peleg, "for in his days the earth was divided" (Genesis 10:25). His name is generally connected with a Hebrew root meaning "small," "little," or "younger." That derivation is probable rather than certain, and Scripture itself never explains the name. Joktan appears only in the…

h3370.sum: Jokshan was a son of Abraham by Keturah, the woman Abraham took after the account of Sarah's death and Isaac's marriage. He was the second listed of Keturah's six sons, and Scripture remembers him chiefly as the father of Sheba and Dedan, names later tied to the trading peoples of Arabia (Genesis 25:2–3; 1 Chronicles 1:32). The meaning of his name is uncertain. It is often connected with a Hebrew verb meaning "to…

h3372.g: afraid, Awesome, awesome, because, Fear, fear, feared, fearing, made, must
h3372.sum: Yârêʼ is the ordinary Hebrew verb for fear, and it covers the whole range of that experience. It describes a soldier shaking before an enemy, a guilty man hiding from God, a worshiper bowing in reverent awe, and a child honoring his parents. Some forms describe what causes fear, so the same word can call God, His deeds, or His coming day "awesome," "terrible," or "dreadful." The word never shrinks to mere…

h3381.g: Bring, bring, brings, brought, came, Come, come, comes, coming, down, Go, go, goes, going, gone, run, take, taken, took, went
h3381.sum: The Hebrew verb yârad means to go down or come down. It can describe a traveler heading downhill, rain falling from the sky, tears running down a face, or a body being lowered into the grave. Because Canaan is hill country, Israelites "went down" to Egypt, to the sea, and to the Jordan valley. As a result, the word appears constantly in the travels of Abraham, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Samson, and David.

h3382.sum: Jared is a name the Hebrew Bible gives to two different men. The better known is the patriarch before the Flood: the son of Mahalalel, the father of Enoch, and the sixth generation from Adam through Seth (Genesis 5:15–20; 1 Chronicles 1:2). The second is a much later man of Judah, called "the father of Gedor" in a difficult genealogy of that tribe (1 Chronicles 4:18). The name comes from the Hebrew verb yarad , "to…

h3389.sum: Jerusalem is the city God chose for His name. It first appears in Scripture as a Canaanite city in the hill country (Joshua 10:1), and it was the Jebusite stronghold that David later captured (2 Samuel 5:6–7). David made it his capital, and Solomon built the temple there. For centuries it was the place where Israel's kings reigned and the tribes went up to worship. The origin and meaning of the name are not certain.…

h3392.sum: Jerah was a son of Joktan in the line of Shem. His name appears only twice in Scripture, both times in a list of Joktan's thirteen sons (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20). The name means "moon" or "month." In form it is the same as the Hebrew word for "month," and it is closely related to the word for "moon." Jerah is best understood as both a man and the ancestor of a people. Genesis places Joktan's descendants in…

h3407.sum: The Hebrew word yᵉrîyʻâh means a curtain: a long panel of woven fabric or goats' hair that could be joined with other panels to form the walls and roof of a tent. Most of its uses describe the curtains of the wilderness tabernacle, the movable tent where God chose to live among Israel. The inner curtains were fine linen woven with cherubim. Over them lay a coarse tent of goats' hair. Fifty gold clasps joined the…

h3409.sum: The Hebrew word yârêk means thigh or hip , the strong upper leg and the joint that bears a person's weight. Scripture uses it for the body itself: where a soldier straps his sword, where a priest's linen covering must reach, and where a grieving person strikes himself in shame. Because the thigh is also a modest way of speaking of the body's power to father children, the word can stand for a man's descendants. By…

h3435.sum: Ishbak was one of the six sons Abraham fathered through Keturah, whose family Genesis records after the account of Sarah's burial and Isaac's marriage. He is named only twice in Scripture, both times in a list of his brothers (Genesis 25:2; 1 Chronicles 1:32). Nothing he said or did is recorded. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Some connect it to a root meaning "to leave" or "to forsake," but that link is…

h345.sum: Aiah is the name of two different men in the Old Testament, and neither one ever speaks or acts on the page. The first is a Horite, a son of Zibeon, listed among the original peoples of Mount Seir in the genealogies of Genesis 36:24 and 1 Chronicles 1:40. The second is an Israelite known only as the father of Rizpah, the concubine of King Saul (2 Samuel 3:7; 21:8, 10, 11). The name is Hebrew and means "bird of…

h3458.sum: Ishmael is a Hebrew name meaning "God hears" or "God will hear." Six different men carry it in the Old Testament, and two of them stand out. The first and most important is Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarah. He was born when Abram and Sarai tried to obtain God's promised heir by their own arrangement. God gave him his name before he was born, because "the LORD has heard your…

h3463.sum: The Hebrew word yâshên describes someone who is asleep: the sleeping one, the sleeper. It appears only nine times in the Old Testament. Each time it pictures the same condition: a person who is unaware, inactive, and unable to protect what is close at hand. A king sleeps while his enemy stands over him with a spear. A mother sleeps while her child is taken from her side. A baker sleeps through the night while his…

h3465.sum: The Hebrew word yâshân means "old" in the sense of something that has lasted from an earlier time: grain kept from last year's harvest, fruit stored up for later, a gate or a pool that has stood in Jerusalem for generations. Scripture never uses it for elderly people or for the ancient ages of eternity. It describes things that have survived, been stored, or been inherited.

h3478.sum: Israel is the name God gave to Jacob, son of Isaac and grandson of Abraham. Through his twelve sons it became the name of an entire people. Across the Old Testament, "Israel" can mean the patriarch himself, the twelve-tribe nation descended from him, the land God gave them, and, after Solomon's kingdom split, the ten northern tribes as distinct from Judah. The prophets can also address Judah and Jerusalem as Israel,…

h349.sum: The Hebrew word ʼêyk means "how?" It is a small word, yet it often appears at the moments when people reach the end of themselves. Judah uses it when he cannot face his father without Benjamin. Moses uses it when the people are too heavy to carry. Israel uses it when stronger nations seem impossible to overcome. Exiles use it when their guilt seems to leave them no future: "how can we then live?" (Ezekiel 33:10). In…

h3506.sum: Ithran is the name of two different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused. The first is a Horite, a son of Dishon (Genesis 36:26; 1 Chronicles 1:41) among "the sons of Seir the Horite who inhabited the land" (Genesis 36:20). The Horites lived in the mountains of Seir before the descendants of Esau took the region, which came to be called Edom (Deuteronomy 2:12). The second is an Israelite of the…

h3509.sum: Jetheth was one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. He appears only twice in Scripture, in the list of Edomite chiefs in Genesis 36:40 and in its repetition in 1 Chronicles 1:51. Genesis presents these chiefs "according to their families and their places," so the name Jetheth seems to stand for both a clan leader and the clan or district that carried his name somewhere in the region of Mount Seir.…

h3518.sum: The Hebrew verb kâbâh means to go out or to put out . It is used for a fire or a lamp, either one that dies for lack of fuel or one that someone deliberately extinguishes. Scripture uses it for the altar fire in the tabernacle, the lamps in God's house, and a household hearth. It also uses the word for a family line, a king's life, and the burning of God's judgment. Most of its uses are negative. Some fires "shall…

h354.sum: The Hebrew word ʼayâl means a deer, specifically the male deer or stag. In the law of Moses the deer is clean wild game that Israel could eat freely at home. On Solomon's table it is a sign of a prosperous kingdom. Most memorably, the Bible's poets and prophets use the deer as a picture of the human soul and of God's people. The deer is a creature that cannot live without water and pasture, that runs and leaps with…

h355.sum: The Hebrew word ʼayâlâh means a doe, or female deer, the graceful wild animal of the hills and forests of Israel. This word never appears in a sacrifice or a food law. Nearly every time she appears, she is a picture. Her sure footing on steep, rocky heights, her hidden birthing in the wild, and her shy, easily startled nature each become a way of seeing something about God and the people He cares for.

h3563.sum: Kôwç is the ordinary Hebrew word for a cup, the vessel a king, a servant, or a poor man in his hut would lift to his lips. Scripture lets this everyday object carry a great deal. Someone who hands you a cup has decided what you will drink, so the cup became a natural picture of a person's lot in life, the portion measured out and placed in a person's hands. David can say of the Lord, "You are the portion of my…

h3568.sum: The Bible uses Cush for different people and lands, whose histories should be distinguished. Most often it names the land and people south of Egypt along the upper Nile, roughly ancient Nubia and today's northern Sudan, which the NKJV usually renders "Ethiopia." The same name belongs to a son of Ham and grandson of Noah, the ancestor listed first among Ham's sons and the father of Nimrod (Genesis 10:6–8). It also…

h3602.sum: The Hebrew word kâkâh is a small pointing word meaning thus , so , in this manner or such . It points to something specific: a way of acting, a condition, a spoken plan, or a set of events. The word has no theological content of its own. Its weight comes from what it points to, and it points to some remarkable things. God tells Israel exactly how to eat the first Passover, dressed and ready to leave Egypt. A prophet…

h366.sum: The Hebrew adjective ʼâyôm describes something so overwhelming that it stops a person in their tracks. English translations render it "terrible" or "awesome." The word occurs 3 times in 3 verses of the Hebrew Bible, and the settings could hardly be further apart. Habakkuk uses it for the Babylonian army sweeping toward Judah as God's instrument of judgment. The Song of Solomon uses it twice for the bride, who is…

h3667.sum: Canaan is first a man and then a land. Genesis introduces him as the son of Ham and grandson of Noah, the one on whom Noah pronounced a curse after Ham's shameful act in the tent (Genesis 9:18–27). His descendants, including Sidon, Heth, and the peoples later known as Jebusites, Amorites, Hivites and others, settled the territory between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea. That territory took his name. The…

h3695.sum: Casluhim is the name of an ancient people listed among the descendants of Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt, in the family tree of nations that grew from Noah's sons after the flood. The name appears only twice in the Bible, in Genesis 10:14 and in the repeated genealogy of 1 Chronicles 1:12. The Casluhim never appear in a story, a prophecy, or a psalm. What makes them matter is the short note attached to their…

h3701.sum: The Hebrew word keçeph means "silver." Because Israel and its neighbors usually paid by weighing out pieces of precious metal, the same word also served as the everyday word for "money," "price," or "payment." So keçeph appears wherever people buy, sell, give, steal, or trust. It shows up in Abraham's purchase of a burial cave, in Joseph's sale into slavery, in the Tabernacle and the Temple, in royal treasuries, in…

h3709.g: both, hand, handles, hands, palm, palms, pan, pans, paws, sole, soles
h3709.sum: The Hebrew word kaph names the flat or hollowed part of something. Most often it means the palm of the hand or the sole of the foot. The same shape explains its other uses: the socket of a hip joint, a handful of flour, an animal's paw, and the small gold pans that held incense in the tabernacle and temple. The NKJV usually translates it "hand" or "hands," but the word describes the open, cupped surface of the hand:…

h3724.sum: The Hebrew word kôpher most often means a ransom: the price paid so that a life under sentence may go free. Scripture also uses it for the pitch that sealed Noah's ark, for country villages, for the fragrant henna plant, and, in its darkest use, for a bribe that blinds a judge. The ransom passages carry the weight of the word. In ordinary life a ransom could settle a real liability, as when an ox owner paid "to…

h3732.sum: Kaphtôrîy is the Hebrew name for the people of Caphtor, called the "Caphtorim" in the NKJV. It appears only three times in the Old Testament. Two of these are in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:14, repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:12), which lists the Caphtorim among the descendants of Mizraim, the ancestor of Egypt, and places them close to the Philistines. The third is a short historical note in Deuteronomy 2:23, which…

h376.g: anyone, anyone’s, Each, each, Everyone, everyone, Husband, husband, husbands, husband’s, Man, man, man’s, O, one
h376.sum: The Hebrew word ʼîysh is the Old Testament's ordinary word for "man." It usually means a particular male person, often a husband. It also works as a simple everyday word for "each" or "anyone," marking out the individual within a group. Because it is so common, it appears in almost every kind of biblical setting: family stories, laws, battle reports, proverbs, and prophecy.

h3763.sum: Cheran was a Horite, one of the original inhabitants of Mount Seir, the rugged highland south of the Dead Sea that later became the land of Edom. He appears only in two parallel genealogies, Genesis 36:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:41. Both name him last among the four sons of Dishon within the Horite clan genealogy; this Dishon is most naturally read as the chief who was a son of Seir. The meaning of his name is uncertain.…

h3794.sum: Kittîy is the Hebrew name for Kittim, a people descended from Javan, and for the island of Cyprus where they settled. Over time the name came to stand for the distant western coastlands of the Mediterranean, the sea peoples and naval powers beyond the horizon of Israel's world. The NKJV renders the same Hebrew word two ways. It keeps "Kittim" in the genealogies of Genesis and 1 Chronicles and uses "Cyprus" in the…

h3796.sum: The Hebrew word kôthel means "wall," specifically the wall of a house. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 2:9, where the bride, waiting inside her home, says of the one she loves: "Behold, he stands behind our wall; He is looking through the windows, Gazing through the lattice." This is a household wall, the ordinary boundary between the inside of a home and the world outside. It is not a…

h3800.sum: The Hebrew word kethem means gold, specifically the finest and most prized gold the ancient world knew. It appears only nine times in the Old Testament, always in poetry and prophecy. Several of those uses tie it to Ophir or Uphaz, distant places famous for their gold. The common Hebrew word for gold furnished the tabernacle and filled royal treasuries, but kethem is the word poets reached for when they needed the…

h3818.sum: Lo-Ammi was the third child born to Gomer, the wife of the prophet Hosea, in the northern kingdom of Israel during the eighth century BC. His name is Hebrew for "Not my people," and God Himself chose it. When the boy was born, the Lord told Hosea, "Call his name Lo-Ammi, For you are not My people, And I will not be your God" (Hosea 1:9). Each time the family called the child, the nation heard God's verdict on years…

h3820.g: heart, hearted, hearts, heart’s, Leb, own
h3820.sum: Lêb is the Old Testament's main word for the heart, and it covers far more than the English word usually does. A modern reader thinks of the heart as feelings, set against the "head." A Hebrew reader made no such split. The heart was where a person thought, understood, decided, desired, grieved, and rejoiced. That is why the NKJV sometimes renders lêb as "mind," "understanding," or "will," and why Proverbs describes…

h3823.sum: The Hebrew verb lâbab is built from the ordinary Old Testament word for "heart." It appears only five times, and those few uses carry two very different meanings. In Job and the Song of Solomon, it describes something happening to a person's heart. In one case, a foolish man would have to "get a heart" and become wise. In the other, a bridegroom confesses that his bride has captured his heart completely: "You have…

h3824.sum: The Hebrew word lêbâb means "heart," but the Bible's heart is far more than the place where feelings live. It is the inner control center of a person: where we think, remember, decide, fear, take courage, worship, and give our loyalty. When Moses tells Israel to love the LORD "with all your heart," he is claiming the whole inner life for God, including attention, intentions, and allegiance. Scripture uses this word…

h3828.sum: The Hebrew word lᵉbônâh names frankincense. Frankincense is a costly, sweet-smelling resin that Israel imported from distant lands such as Sheba. In the tabernacle it was one of the four ingredients of the holy incense. It was also laid on the grain offering and on the Bread of the Presence. When the priest burned it, it rose as "a sweet aroma to the LORD" and served as a "memorial" before Him (Leviticus 2:2; 24:7).…

h3842.sum: The Hebrew word lᵉbânâh means moon . It is a rare, poetic name for the moon that pictures it as the white one , the pale light that rules the night sky. Ordinary Hebrew had another word for the moon, the one tied to months and calendars. Scripture uses lᵉbânâh only three times, and each time the moon appears beside the sun at its most beautiful and most glorious. In the Song of Solomon the bride is "fair as the…

h3853.sum: Lehabim is the name of an ancient people descended from Mizraim, the biblical name for Egypt, who was a son of Ham. The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the same line of the "Table of Nations": "Mizraim begot Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim" (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). It carries no theological meaning of its own. It names a family of peoples who settled in and around the Nile Valley…

h3865.sum: Lud is first a person and then a people. Genesis names him as a son of Shem, listed with his brothers Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, and Aram (Genesis 10:22; 1 Chronicles 1:17). The prophets later use the same name for a distant nation known for its soldiers, and English translations often render it "Lydia." Since ancient times that nation has been identified with the Lydians of western Asia Minor, though Scripture itself…

h3866.sum: Lûwdîy is the Hebrew name for the Ludim, an ancient people whom Scripture places in the family of Egypt. The word appears only three times. Two are in the great list of nations, where "Mizraim begot Ludim" (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). The third is in Jeremiah's prophecy against Egypt, where the NKJV renders the word "Lydians" and describes them as the warriors "who handle and bend the bow" (Jeremiah 46:9).…

h3871.sum: The Hebrew word lûwach means a flat slab or board, a surface that can be written on or built with. Scripture uses it for ship planks, altar boards, and decorative bronze plates. It is best known, though, for the two tablets of stone on which God wrote the Ten Commandments "with the finger of God" (Exodus 31:18). The story of those tablets includes some of the most important moments in the Old Testament. God wrote…

h3877.sum: Lotan was a chief of the Horites, the people who lived in the mountain country of Seir before the descendants of Esau took it over. He is named first among the sons of Seir the Horite (Genesis 36:20; 1 Chronicles 1:38), and his own sons were Hori and Hemam, called Homam in Chronicles. The meaning of his name is not certain. It probably comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to wrap" or "to cover," the same root behind…

h3884.sum: This Hebrew word opens a door onto something that never happened. It introduces a condition contrary to fact, usually in the past: "If this had not been so…" The sentence that follows describes the result that would have come, and that result is almost always disaster. The NKJV renders it "unless," "if… not," or "were it not that." Most often the speaker is looking back with relief or gratitude: Israel would have…

h3885.g: dwell, Lodge, lodge, lodged, night, remain, spend, spent, Stay, stayed
h3885.sum: This Hebrew word most often describes stopping for the night: a traveler looking for shelter, an army making camp, a guest received into a home. Abraham's servant asks for room to lodge, and Ruth tells Naomi, "wherever you lodge, I will lodge." From that ordinary picture the poets and prophets draw vivid language. Weeping may "endure for a night" but must leave at morning (Psalm 30:5). The one who dwells in God's…

h3895.sum: The Hebrew word lᵉchîy means the jaw or cheek, the lower side of the face of a person or an animal. It is an ordinary body word, but Scripture uses it at some of its most telling moments. A cheek can be struck in contempt, wet with tears, or admired in love. A jaw can be a weapon in Samson's hand, a predator's strength that God breaks, the place where a yoke rests on a working animal, or the place where God sets a…

h39.sum: Abimael is one of the thirteen sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Arphaxad, Salah, and Eber. He appears only twice in Scripture, both times as a single name in a list: once in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:28) and once in the Chronicler's matching genealogy (1 Chronicles 1:22). His name most likely means "My Father is God (El)," though the exact force of the middle syllable is debated. Some scholars…

h3925.g: anyone, Learn, learn, learned, taught, Teach, teach, teachers, teaches, teaching, trained, trains
h3925.sum: The Hebrew verb lâmad is the Old Testament's main word for learning and teaching. In one form it means "to learn," and in another it means "to teach" or "to train." Scripture uses it for a soldier whose hands have been drilled for battle, a young animal broken to the yoke, and a child learning God's commandments at home. Biblical learning is never just storing information. A person has learned something when it has…

h3929.sum: Lamech is the name of two different men who lived before the Flood. They stand at turning points in two very different family lines. The first Lamech belongs to the family of Cain, and he is the seventh generation from Adam through that line (Genesis 4:18–24). He took two wives, fathered the founders of herding, music, and metalworking, and then composed a song boasting that he had killed a young man for wounding…

h3950.g: Gather, gather, gathered, glean, gleaned, up
h3950.sum: The Hebrew verb lâqaṭ means to gather, pick up, or glean. It describes collecting scattered things from the ground one piece at a time: stones for a heap, sticks for a fire, arrows after target practice, stalks of grain dropped behind the reapers. Scripture uses the word most often in two places. In Exodus 16, Israel goes out each morning to gather manna. In Leviticus and Ruth, the poor glean what harvesters leave…

h3956.g: bay, language, languages, tongue, tongues, wedge
h3956.sum: The Hebrew word lâshôwn means "tongue." Most often it names the tongue as the organ of speech. In Scripture, though, the tongue is rarely neutral. It shows what is in the heart. In the Psalms and Proverbs it can be a sword, an arrow, or a serpent's poison, or it can be "choice silver" and a source of healing. The same word can also mean a people's language , and it can describe things shaped like a tongue: a wedge…

h3966.sum: The Hebrew word mᵉʼôd is the Old Testament's ordinary word for "very," "greatly," and "exceedingly." It turns up the volume on whatever it touches: a city's wickedness, a famine's severity, a father's grief, a king's terror, or the greatness of God. On its own it carries no moral weight. It intensifies, and the Bible's writers choose carefully what they intensify. The same word that marks God's verdict on finished…

h398.g: ate, caused, consume, consumed, consumes, consuming, Devour, devour, devoured, devourer, Devouring, devouring, devours, Eat, eat, eaten, eater, Eating, eating, eats, fed, feed, has, have, may
h398.sum: The Hebrew verb ʼâkal is the Old Testament's ordinary word for eating. It is used for a traveler's meal, a harvest supper, a king's table, and the food God gives His people. The same verb also describes what fire, the sword, wild animals, and locusts do. In those settings the NKJV translates it "consume" or "devour." One word covers both nourishment and destruction: you either eat, or you are eaten.

h4014.sum: Mibzar was one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. He is named only twice, in the closing list of Edomite chiefs in Genesis 36:42 and again in the Chronicler's copy of that list in 1 Chronicles 1:53. The name means "fortress" or "fortified place." It is the same word Hebrew uses for a stronghold or walled city. Genesis says these chiefs were listed "according to their families and their places"…

h4017.sum: Mibsam is the name of two different men in the Old Testament genealogies. The first, and better known, is the fourth-listed son of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He is listed among the twelve sons who became tribal chiefs in the Arabian wilderness (Genesis 25:13; 1 Chronicles 1:29). The second is a descendant of Simeon, the son of Shallum and father of Mishma, whose family lived on Israel's southern frontier (1…

h4022.sum: The Hebrew word meged describes the very best of something: its choicest, most excellent part. The NKJV translates it as "precious things," "precious," or "pleasant." Scripture never uses it for gold, jewels, or anything made by human hands. It always describes the finest gifts of the living world, such as the dew of heaven, the deep springs, the harvest ripened by the sun and the months, the riches of the ancient…

h4025.sum: Magdiel was one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother. His name appears only twice in Scripture: in the closing roster of Edomite chiefs in Genesis 36:43 and in the Chronicler's retelling of that list in 1 Chronicles 1:54. The name is a compound of a Hebrew word for "excellence" or "choice thing" and El , "God," so it most likely means "choice gift of God" or "preciousness of…

h4026.sum: The Hebrew word migdâl means a tower, a tall structure built to raise people above the ground around them. In the Old Testament it names city towers where frightened people fled during a siege, watchtowers where a guard could see trouble coming, towers in vineyards and pastures that protected the harvest and the flock, and once the wooden platform from which Ezra read God's Law to the returned exiles.

h4031.sum: Magog appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, yet few names travel farther. It begins as the name of the second-listed son of Japheth and grandson of Noah, listed among the peoples who spread across the earth after the Flood (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). Centuries later, Ezekiel uses it for a distant northern land whose ruler, Gog, leads a vast army against God's restored people (Ezekiel 38–39). Finally,…

h4043.sum: The Hebrew word mâgên means a shield. It usually means the smaller, hand-held shield a soldier raised and moved to turn aside blows in close fighting. Scripture uses it for real equipment: Solomon's gold shields, the weapons of invading armies, and the gear of Nehemiah's builders. It also uses the word in some of the Bible's most personal confessions of faith. The first time the word appears, God tells Abram, "Do…

h4074.sum: Mâday names two closely linked things in the Hebrew Bible.
