First, it is Madai, a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah, listed among the founding peoples in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). Second, and far more often, it is Media and the Medes, the people and land in the mountains of what is now northwestern Iran. Over time the Medes became a major world power and later partners with Persia. The…

h4080.sum: Midian is the name of a son of Abraham, of the people descended from him, and of the desert land where they lived, chiefly east of the Gulf of Aqaba and ranging across the wilderness south and east of Canaan. The name most likely comes from a Hebrew root meaning "strife," "contention," or "judgment." That derivation is probable rather than certain, and Scripture never builds a lesson on it. Midian was born to…

h4091.sum: Medan was one of the six sons born to Abraham through Keturah, whose marriage Genesis records after the account of Sarah's death. He is named only in two family lists, Genesis 25:2 and 1 Chronicles 1:32. His name is usually connected with a Hebrew word meaning "strife" or "contention," related to a root that means to judge or contend. That meaning is a probable derivation, not a certain one, and Scripture never…

h4095.sum: The Hebrew word madrêgâh names a steep place: a sheer cliff, a rocky ledge, or high rough ground that few can reach. It appears only twice in the Old Testament, and the two uses could hardly be more different. In Song of Solomon 2:14 the beloved calls to his bride as a dove hidden "in the secret places of the cliff," safe in rock no predator can climb. In Ezekiel 38:20 God's presence comes in judgment, and "the…

h4100.g: How, how, long, many, often, What, what, Whatever, whatever, Why, why
h4100.sum: The Hebrew word mâh is the Old Testament's basic way of asking "what?" In the NKJV it also appears as "why," "how," and "whatever," because this one word can ask about a thing, a reason, or a degree. Often the speaker is not looking for information. When God asks Cain, "What have you done?" He already knows the answer. The question presses Cain to face his deed.

h4105.sum: Mehetabel is a Hebrew name meaning "God does good" or "God benefits." Two different people in Scripture bear it, living many centuries apart. The first is a queen of Edom, the wife of King Hadar (spelled Hadad in Chronicles). Genesis 36:39 and 1 Chronicles 1:50 both name her among the early kings of Esau's descendants. She is the only royal wife mentioned in that list, and the record also names two generations of…

h4111.sum: Mahalalel is the name of two men in the Old Testament. The better known is the patriarch of Genesis 5. He was the son of Cainan, the father of Jared, and the fifth generation from Adam through Seth. The name means "Praise of God" or "God's praise." It joins the Hebrew word for praise with El , God. Scripture records only his birth, his fatherhood, his 895 years, and his death. Yet his place in the line running from…

h4124.sum: Moab is the name of a man, the nation descended from him, and the land that nation occupied east of the Dead Sea. The first Moab was the son of Lot by his elder daughter, born in the cave after the destruction of Sodom (Genesis 19:37). His descendants became a settled kingdom across the Jordan from Israel. Its territory gave its name to the "plains of Moab," where Israel camped before entering Canaan. The name is…

h4191.g: being, cause, dead, death, die, died, dies, has, Kill, kill, killed, killing, kills, put, slays, surely
h4191.sum: Mûwth is the ordinary Hebrew verb for dying. It describes a person or animal coming to the end of life, and in other forms it means to kill, execute, or put to death. Scripture uses it in genealogies, battle reports, courtroom laws, priestly warnings, and the laments of Job and Ecclesiastes. Wherever life ends in the Old Testament, this word is usually present.

h4195.sum: Môwthâr is a Hebrew word for what is left over: the surplus, gain, or advantage that remains when the account is settled. It appears only three times in the Old Testament, all in the wisdom books. In Proverbs it names the real "profit" and "plenty" that come from honest labor and careful planning, set against the "poverty" that follows empty talk and hasty shortcuts. In Ecclesiastes the same word takes on a heavier…

h4197.sum: The Hebrew word mezeg means "mixture" and refers to wine that has been blended or prepared, rendered by the NKJV as "blended beverage." It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:2, where the bride is praised in the language of a royal banquet: "Your navel is a rounded goblet; It lacks no blended beverage." Prepared wine of this kind was a drink for feasts and weddings, so the image speaks of delight,…

h4199.sum: Mizzah was a grandson of Esau, the fourth-listed son of Reuel and Basemath's grandson, and he became one of the chiefs of Edom. His name appears only three times, all in family records (Genesis 36:13, 17; 1 Chronicles 1:37). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Strong's tentatively connects it to an unused root meaning to faint with fear, but the evidence is too thin to build anything on, and it may simply have…

h420.sum: Eldaah was a grandson of Abraham through Keturah. He was the last of the five sons of Midian listed in Genesis 25:4 and again in 1 Chronicles 1:33. His name joins El , "God," with a second element whose root is debated. It probably means "God has known," though some scholars read it as "God has called" or "God of knowledge." No other person in Scripture bears this name, and he does nothing in the biblical record…

h4210.sum: The Hebrew word mizmôwr means a psalm, a song set to music. The NKJV translates it "Psalm," and every one of its occurrences is in the Book of Psalms, always in the heading above a psalm, never inside the poem itself. When a heading reads "A Psalm of David," this is the word at work. It tells the reader what kind of text follows: a composition meant to be sung, most likely with instruments.

h425.sum: Elah is a Hebrew name meaning "terebinth," a large, long-lived tree common in the land of Israel and sometimes rendered "oak" in English Bibles. The name belongs to one famous place and several different people, and keeping them separate is essential. The best known is the Valley of Elah, a broad valley in the foothills of Judah where Saul's army faced the Philistines and young David killed Goliath (1 Samuel 17:2,…

h4261.sum: The Hebrew word machmâd names something that draws the heart and the eye: a prized possession, a cherished person, or anything that is a delight to look at. The NKJV translates it as "pleasant things," "valuables," "precious possessions," "darlings," "the desire of your eyes," and, in one memorable line, "altogether lovely." The word describes the thing loved rather than the act of loving it. In itself the word is…

h4284.g: design, own, plan, Plans, plans, purposes, thoughts
h4284.sum: Machăshâbâh is the Hebrew word for what the mind produces: a thought, an intention, a plan, a scheme, or a skilled design. It describes the inner work of thinking something through before it becomes action. Scripture uses it for the corrupt thoughts of the human heart before the flood, for Haman's plot to destroy the Jews, and for the artistic designs God's Spirit gave Bezalel for the tabernacle. Most strikingly, it…

h4308.sum: Matred was a member of an Edomite family remembered in Scripture only through a royal marriage. When Hadar (spelled Hadad in Chronicles) became king of Edom, the record names his wife Mehetabel as "the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab" (Genesis 36:39; compare 1 Chronicles 1:50). Matred is most often understood to be Mehetabel's mother, though the wording has been read in more than one way. The name is…

h4314.sum: Mezahab is named only in the royal record of Edom, as the ancestor of Mehetabel, wife of Hadar (called Hadad in Chronicles), the eighth king listed in Edom (Genesis 36:39; 1 Chronicles 1:50). His name means "waters of gold," a Hebrew compound of the words for "waters" and "gold." Scripture never explains why he bore the name, and it records nothing he did. He appears in Edom's king-list, which Genesis introduces as…

h4325.sum: Mayim is the ordinary Hebrew word for water. It names the water a traveler drinks, the water a priest washes with, the rain that falls on the fields, the river Israel crossed, and the deep that covered the earth before God spoke light into being. The word itself means nothing more than "water." Scripture, however, returns to it so often and in so many settings that water becomes one of the Bible's richest pictures…

h4339.sum: The Hebrew word mêyshâr describes what is straight, level and even. It names a path with no bend in it, a judgment that leans toward no one, and speech that says exactly what is true. The NKJV renders it "uprightness," "equity," "uprightly," "right things," and even "smoothly." That last rendering shows the word's concrete root: wine that slides down with nothing to hinder it.

h4421.sum: The Hebrew word milchâmâh is the Old Testament's ordinary word for war and battle. It names real armies, real weapons and real bloodshed: a single day's fighting, a long campaign between rival kingdoms, or the soldier's skill in combat. It appears from Abraham's rescue of Lot to the prophets' visions of the last days, and it is especially frequent in the stories of Israel's kings.

h4428.g: King, king, Kings, kings, King’s, king’s, Milcom, O
h4428.sum: Melek is the ordinary Hebrew word for "king." It names the man who sits at the top of a people's authority. That might be the ruler of a small Canaanite town, the emperor of Assyria or Persia, or a son of David on the throne in Jerusalem. The same word is also used of the LORD Himself. When the psalmist sings, "The LORD is King forever and ever" (Psalm 10:16), he uses the same word the historians use for Pharaoh and…

h4436.sum: The Hebrew word malkâh means queen . It is the feminine partner of the ordinary Hebrew word for king , and in Scripture it names two kinds of royal women. One is a ruler in her own right, like the queen of Sheba, who governs her land and travels with her own wealth. The other is a king's chief wife, like Vashti and Esther in the Persian court, who holds the highest rank among the royal women but still lives under…

h4477.sum: The Hebrew word mamtaq means "sweetness" or "something sweet." It appears only twice in the Old Testament, and the NKJV translates it "sweet" both times. The two passages could hardly be more different. In Nehemiah 8:10, the word names the sweet drinks of a holy feast. In Song of Solomon 5:16, it describes the mouth of a beloved bridegroom. In both verses the word is plural, as if one sweetness were not enough.

h4480.g: any, More, more, one, portion, Since, since, Some, some, than
h4480.w: From, Out Of, Of, Because Of
h4480.sum: The Hebrew word min is one of the small, ordinary words that hold the Old Testament together. It usually means "from" or "out of," and it answers the question "Where did this come from?" Depending on its setting, it can also mean "because of," "since," "among," "some of," or "more than." It tells where something starts, what caused it, what it has been separated from, or what larger whole it belongs to.

h4496.sum: Mᵉnûwchâh is the Hebrew word for rest: a settled, secure condition, or the place where that settled life is found. It describes more than a break from work. A young widow finds it in a husband's home, Israel finds it in the land God promised, and the soul finds it beside the "still waters" of Psalm 23. Most strikingly, God Himself speaks of a resting place. David wanted to build Him a "house of rest," and in Psalm…

h4506.sum: Manahath is a name the Bible uses in two ways. It belongs to a Horite man, a son of Shobal, who lived among the original inhabitants of Mount Seir before Esau's descendants took that land (Genesis 36:23; 1 Chronicles 1:40). It is also the name of a town or clan district in Israel. In Judah's genealogy, the "Manahethites" are counted among the families descended from Shobal and Salma, grandsons of Caleb son of Hezron…

h4514.sum: The Hebrew word manʻûwl names the bolt or lock that fastens a door shut. It is a small, practical word that appears only a handful of times in Scripture, and it appears in two very different settings. In Nehemiah 3, Jerusalem's gates are rebuilt one by one, and the record keeps noting that the builders hung the doors "with its bolts and bars." In Song of Solomon 5:5, the same word describes the lock on a bedroom…

h4524.sum: The Hebrew word mêçab describes what surrounds something: the area around a city, a ring of carvings on a wall, clouds circling through the sky, a circle of enemies, or the circle of guests around a king. The NKJV translates it "around," "about," "surround," and once "table." Because the English words differ, readers can easily miss that all five uses share one picture: something enclosed by what stands around it.

h4557.sum: The Hebrew word miçpâr means "number," the count or total of something. Scripture uses it for an army roster, the days of a festival, the months of a man's life, or the years of an exile. Two common phrases stretch its range. People who are "men of number" are so few they can be counted at a glance, which is why the NKJV often translates the phrase "few." Something "without number" cannot be counted at all, and the…

h4570.sum: Maʻgâl is a Hebrew word for a track or worn path, the kind of established course left in the ground by repeated travel. In the historical books it names the circular camp of Saul's army. In the Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah it becomes a picture of a person's course of life. Most English readers know it from one of the best-loved lines in Scripture: "He leads me in the paths of righteousness For His name's sake"…

h4585.sum: The Hebrew word mᵉʻôwnâh means a dwelling, but it is usually a wild one. Most of its uses describe a lair, the den where lions and other beasts lie down, hide, and rest. It names a place of retreat that no one dares to disturb. Because the word appears only nine times, each use stands out, and its rugged sense carries into the passages where it is applied to people and to God.

h4592.sum: The Hebrew word mᵉʻaṭ means "little" or "few." It measures something as small compared with something larger. That something may be a quantity, such as a little water, a few people, or a small remnant. It may be a span of time ("a little while," "soon"), a degree ("almost," "scarcely"), or a matter of importance ("a small thing"). The NKJV uses more than a dozen English words to translate it, which shows how often…

h4639.g: business, deed, deeds, thing, work, worked, working, workmanship, works
h4639.sum: The Hebrew word maʻăseh means a "work": something done or made. It can describe the woven curtains of the tabernacle, a shepherd's daily occupation, a person's moral deeds, an idol carved by a craftsman, or the heavens God set in place with His fingers. The word names the real result an action leaves behind. Whether that result is glorious or shameful depends on whose hands made it and for what purpose.

h464.sum: Eliphaz is the name of two different men in the Old Testament, and both belong to the world of Edom. The first is Esau's firstborn son by his wife Adah. His sons became chiefs of Edom, and through his concubine Timna he became the father of Amalek, whose descendants were Israel's bitter enemy for centuries (Genesis 36:10–12; 1 Chronicles 1:35–36). The second is Eliphaz the Temanite, the first and leading speaker…

h4672.g: come, delivered, find, finding, Finds, finds, Found, found, had, has, have, meet, met
h4672.sum: The Hebrew verb mâtsâʼ means to find . It covers the ordinary experience of coming upon what was sought or hidden, such as a lost donkey, a stolen cup, or water in the desert. It also means to meet someone, to have enough of something, or simply to be found , meaning to be present. Scripture uses this everyday word for some of its weightiest realities. Noah "found grace in the eyes of the LORD." Moses promised…

h4714.sum: Egypt, in Hebrew Mitsrayim , is the ancient land and nation of the Nile valley southwest of Canaan. It is one of the most frequently named places in the Old Testament. The same Hebrew name first appears as Mizraim, a son of Ham, whose descendants are listed among the nations in Genesis 10. The name is commonly explained as meaning "double straits" or "two distresses." Its dual-looking ending is often linked to the…

h473.sum: Elishah appears only three times in the Bible, but those three verses reach from the scattering of the nations after the Flood to the prophetic lament over Tyre. In Genesis 10:4 and 1 Chronicles 1:7, Elishah is the first-named son of Javan, a grandson of Japheth and great-grandson of Noah. His line is among those from whom "the coastland peoples of the Gentiles were separated into their lands" (Genesis 10:5). By…

h4758.sum: The Hebrew word marʼeh means "appearance" or "sight," the way something looks when it is seen. Scripture uses it for ordinary things: Rachel's beauty, Joseph's good looks, the fat and gaunt cows in Pharaoh's dream, and a sore on the skin that a priest had to examine. It also describes the most overwhelming sights a human being has ever been given. The glory of the LORD on Sinai looked "like a consuming fire."…

h4832.sum: The Hebrew noun marpêʼ means healing, health, cure, or remedy. It describes the condition of something that has been made whole again, and Scripture applies it to a sick body, a troubled heart, a strained relationship, and a nation broken under God's judgment. English versions translate it in several ways: "health," "healing," "remedy," "wholesome," "sound," and once, in a conflict with a ruler, "conciliation."

h4840.sum: The Hebrew word merqâch means a spice or perfume, and it carries the sense of fragrance that has been skillfully blended. It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 5:13. There the bride describes the man she loves: "His cheeks are like a bed of spices, Banks of scented herbs." The NKJV translates merqâch as "scented." The word belongs to the family of Hebrew terms for the perfumer's craft. That is the…

h4854.sum: Massa was the seventh-listed of the twelve sons of Ishmael, which makes him a grandson of Abraham through Hagar the Egyptian. Scripture names him only twice, both times in the family record of Ishmael (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30). Like his brothers, he gave his name to a people, one of the "twelve princes according to their nations" who settled in the deserts of northern Arabia (Genesis 25:16). His name is…

h486.sum: Almodad is the first-named son of Joktan in the Table of Nations. Joktan was a son of Eber and a descendant of Shem through Arphaxad and Salah. Almodad appears only twice in Scripture, both times in the same list: "Joktan begot Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah" (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20). The meaning of his name is uncertain. Some interpret it in Hebrew as something like "God is a friend" or "measure of…

h4900.g: away, deferred, Draw, draw, Drawing, draws, drew, follow, gratify, postponed, prolong, prolonged, sounds, stretched, tall
h4900.sum: The Hebrew verb mâshak means to draw , in the sense of pulling something toward yourself or stretching it out. It is an ordinary working word. Brothers pull Joseph up out of a pit, a soldier draws back a bowstring, priests sound a long blast on the ram's horn, and a farmer draws seed out of his bag as he sows. The same word can also stretch time. Hope can be "deferred," God can have "patience" for many years, and a…

h4902.sum: Meshech first appears in Scripture as a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). It then becomes the name of the people descended from him, a distant northern nation usually paired with Tubal. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It sounds like a Hebrew verb meaning "to draw" or "to drag," and some have connected it with drawing a bow. It is more likely the Hebrew form of a foreign…

h4904.sum: The Hebrew word mishkâb means a bed or a place for lying down. It names the couch where people sleep, the sickbed where they suffer, the private bedroom where they speak freely, and, by a natural extension, the act of lying together in sexual union. Poets and prophets also use it for the grave, where the dead are laid to rest. Because the bed is where people are least guarded, Scripture often uses this word to show…

h4908.sum: The Hebrew word mishkân means a dwelling place, the place where someone lives. It can describe ordinary homes and tents, such as the "dwellings" of Israel that Balaam admired from a mountaintop (Numbers 24:5). Most often, though, it names the Tabernacle, the portable sanctuary Israel built in the wilderness so that the LORD could live in the middle of their camp. God said, "Let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may…

h4927.sum: Mishma is the name of two different men in the Bible's family records. The first is the fifth-listed son of Ishmael, a brother of Mibsam, listed among the twelve princes who descended from Abraham through Hagar (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30). The second is a man from the tribe of Simeon, the son (not the brother) of Mibsam and father of Hamuel (1 Chronicles 4:25–26). The name comes from the Hebrew verb shama ,…

h4938.sum: The Hebrew word mishʻênâh means a support, something a person leans on. Most often it is a walking-stick or staff: the stick an injured man uses to walk outside again, the staff an old woman holds as she sits in a Jerusalem street, the staff of a shepherd. Once it means something you cannot hold in your hand. In Isaiah 3:1 it describes the bread and water a city leans on to stay alive.

h4957.sum: Masrekah was a town in ancient Edom, the land settled by Esau's descendants in the mountains of Seir south and east of the Dead Sea. Scripture names it twice, in one narrative notice preserved in two parallel records: "When Hadad died, Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place" (Genesis 36:36; 1 Chronicles 1:47). The name probably means "vineyard" or "place of choice vines." It appears to come from the same Hebrew…

h4966.sum: The Hebrew word mâthôwq means sweet . At its simplest it describes the taste of honey or ripe fruit. Scripture also uses it for anything a person finds deeply pleasant: the sleep of a tired worker, the light of the sun, kind words, and the judgments of the Lord. The word is rare, appearing only about a dozen times, mostly in Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Solomon, with a few striking uses in Judges,…

h4968.sum: Methuselah was the son of Enoch, the father of Lamech, and the grandfather of Noah. He belongs to the line of Seth that Genesis 5 traces from Adam to the Flood. He is best known as the longest-lived person in Scripture: "So all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred and sixty-nine years; and he died" (Genesis 5:27). The meaning of his name is uncertain. Many scholars read it as "man of the dart" or "man of the…

h4994.sum: This small Hebrew word stands behind many of the Old Testament's "please"s, "I pray"s, and persuasive "now"s. It turns a bare command or wish into an appeal. Servants use it before masters, brothers use it with brothers, and worshipers use it before God. Most surprising of all, God uses it with His own people: "Come now, and let us reason together" (Isaiah 1:18). Once you can hear the word, familiar passages sound…

h4998.sum: The Hebrew word nâʼâh means "to be lovely," "to be beautiful," or "to be fitting." It describes beauty that suits its subject and delights the one who sees it. The word appears only three times in the Old Testament, and each use comes at a meaningful moment. In the Song of Solomon a lover tells his beloved that her cheeks are "lovely with ornaments." In Psalm 93 the psalmist declares that "Holiness adorns Your…

h5000.sum: The Hebrew word nâʼveh describes something that is lovely and that belongs where it is. In English it is translated "lovely," "beautiful," "fitting," or "becoming." In the Song of Solomon it describes the beauty of the beloved: her face, her mouth, her whole person. In Proverbs it describes what is suitable, and always in the negative: honor, luxury, and fine speech do not fit a fool. In the Psalms the two ideas…

h5032.sum: Nebaioth was the firstborn son of Ishmael and a grandson of Abraham through Hagar. His name also became the name of the Arabian tribe that descended from him, a pastoral people of the eastern deserts known for their flocks. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It has often been linked to ideas such as "heights," "prominences," or "fruitfulness," but none of these is settled, and Scripture itself offers no…

h505.sum: The Hebrew word ʼeleph means "thousand." Throughout the Old Testament it counts soldiers, sheep, silver and sacrifices. It also names a large family group within a tribe, which the NKJV translates "clan" or "division." Gideon uses this second sense when he protests that "my clan is the weakest in Manasseh" (Judges 6:15). Micah uses it when he calls Bethlehem "little among the thousands of Judah" (Micah 5:2), and…

h5081.sum: The Hebrew word nâdîyb describes a person who is noble. The Old Testament uses that idea in two connected ways. Sometimes it refers to character: a heart that is willing and generous and gives freely without being forced. More often it refers to rank, the "princes" and "nobles" who sat at the top of society. The NKJV translates it as "willing," "generous," "noble," "princes," and "nobles," depending on which of…

h5090.g: away, drive, guide, guiding, lead, leading
h5090.sum: The Hebrew word nâhag is the verb a herdsman uses for moving animals along. It means to drive, lead, or guide, whether the thing being moved is a flock, a team pulling a chariot, a cart, or a line of captives. Jacob drives his livestock toward Canaan. Moses leads Jethro's flock to Horeb. Jehu is recognized from far off because "he drives furiously." Raiders carry off David's family at Ziklag. The word does not…

h5095.sum: The Hebrew verb nâhal means to lead or guide, and it usually describes a leader who takes responsibility for the well-being of those who follow. It appears only ten times in the Old Testament. NKJV renders it "lead," "guide," "guided," and "leads," and in two places it reads "fed" and "ride." Jacob uses it of moving his weary flocks and young children at a pace they could bear. The narrative uses it of Joseph…

h5104.sum: Nâhâr is the ordinary Hebrew word for a river, usually a substantial flowing watercourse. Scripture uses it for the river that watered Eden, for the Nile and its channels, for the rivers of Damascus and Babylon, and especially for the Euphrates, which is so often called simply "the River." In poetry the plural can describe surging waters, so the NKJV sometimes translates it "floods." The same word therefore names…

h5116.sum: The Hebrew word nâveh means a settled place to live. It is often a shepherd's word for the pasture or fold where a flock is brought to rest, and it also describes the homes of people, the dens of wild animals, and the holy dwelling of God. It is the word behind the "green pastures" of Psalm 23, the "good fold" of Ezekiel 34, and the "holy habitation" toward which God led Israel after the Red Sea (Exodus 15:13). It…

h5140.sum: The Hebrew verb nâzal means "to flow." It covers almost every kind of moving water: dew settling on grass, rain dropping from clouds, a mountain stream running cold from the snows of Lebanon, and a torrent splitting out of desert rock. The NKJV translates it with words like "distill," "drop," "flow," "gush," "streams," and "floods." Often the word works as a noun, so that "flowing things" simply become "streams."

h5146.sum: Noah, son of Lamech, stands at the hinge between the world before the Flood and the world after it. He was the tenth generation from Adam through Seth, the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and the man through whom God preserved human life when He judged a world "filled with violence" (Genesis 6:11). His name, Nôach, is generally understood to mean "rest." Genesis explains it with a related-sounding word: at his…

h5148.g: guide, guided, guides, Lead, lead, leads, led
h5148.sum: Nâchâh is the Hebrew verb for leading or guiding someone along a way to a destination. Most often God is the one who leads. He led Israel out of Egypt by the pillar of cloud and fire. He led His flock as a shepherd. And He answers the believer who prays, "Lead me." The word can also describe ordinary human guiding, such as a man escorting his parents to safety, a gift opening a door before great men, or troops…

h5152.sum: Nahor is the name of two men in Abraham's family, and the reader has to keep them apart. The first Nahor was Abraham's grandfather, the son of Serug and the father of Terah, listed in the line from Shem to Abram (Genesis 11:22–25; 1 Chronicles 1:26). Luke's genealogy of Jesus later passes through this man (Luke 3:34). The second Nahor was Abraham's brother, a son of Terah who married his niece Milcah and became,…

h5162.g: comfort, comforted, comforter, comforters, comforts, compassion, regret, regretted, relent, relented, relenting, relents, repent, repented
h5162.sum: Nâcham is a Hebrew verb that carries two meanings English readers might not expect to share one word: "to comfort" and "to relent." Friends use it when they come to sit with the grieving, as Job's friends did. Prophets use it when God turns back from a disaster He has threatened, as He did for Nineveh. Isaiah uses it when God Himself speaks tender words to an exiled people and promises to rebuild their ruins. Both…

h517.sum: The Hebrew word ʼêm is the Old Testament's ordinary word for "mother," the woman who bears, nurses, teaches, and raises a child. Scripture also stretches the word. It can name a grandmother or the first mother of the human race. It can describe a woman like Deborah, who rose to protect God's people, and it can describe a city, or the nation of Israel itself, as the mother of the people who belong to her.

h5184.sum: Nahath is the name of three different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused with one another. The first is a grandson of Esau who became a chief of Edom (Genesis 36:13, 17; 1 Chronicles 1:37). The second is a Kohathite Levite in the ancestry of the prophet Samuel (1 Chronicles 6:26), who appears to be the same man called Toah in 1 Chronicles 6:34 and Tohu in 1 Samuel 1:1. The third is a Levite…

h5197.g: Drip, drip, dripped, Dripping, dropped, prophesy
h5197.sum: The Hebrew word nâṭaph means to drip, drop, or fall in drops. Scripture uses it for rain falling from the heavens, honey and myrrh on the lips, and new wine running down the mountains. Hebrew also uses the word for speech. Words can fall on hearers the way rain falls on ground, so nâṭaph can mean to preach or prophesy. Job's counsel "settled on them as dew" (Job 29:22), and God told Ezekiel to "preach against the…

h5201.sum: The Hebrew verb nâṭar means to keep , to guard , or to maintain . Scripture uses it in two ways. In the Song of Solomon it describes the ordinary work of keeping and tending a vineyard. Everywhere else it describes keeping something inside: holding onto anger or a grudge and refusing to let it go. In that second sense, "keeping" is something a person does. A grudge does not simply linger in the heart. It is held.

h5221.g: attack, attacked, attacks, defeat, defeated, down, had, has, Strike, strike, strikes, striking, struck, thrust, wounded
h5221.sum: The Hebrew verb nâkâh means to strike: to land a blow, whether with a hand, a rod, a sword, or an army. Depending on the setting, it can describe a beating that wounds, a blow that kills, or a military attack that defeats a whole city. It is one of the most common action words in the Old Testament. It fills the battle accounts of Joshua, Samuel, and Kings. It also governs the laws about violence in Exodus and…

h5246.sum: The Hebrew word nâmêr means leopard . It appears only six times in the Old Testament, and the prophets and poets use it for what Israel knew about the animal: it had spots it could not shed, it watched silently from a hidden place, and it struck with terrifying speed. Through this one animal, Scripture shows how deep human sin runs, how unavoidable God's judgment is, and how complete Christ's coming peace will be.

h5248.sum: Nimrod was a descendant of Noah through Ham and Cush. Genesis singles him out as the one who "began to be a mighty one on the earth" (Genesis 10:8). The name is traditionally connected with the Hebrew root marad , "to rebel," and is often explained as "rebel" or "let us rebel." That derivation is a long-standing traditional reading rather than a certain etymology, and Scripture itself never comments on the name's…

h5273.sum: The Hebrew word nâʻîym describes what is pleasant, delightful, or sweet. It can describe the beauty of a thing itself, such as a harp, a bridegroom, or a well-furnished home, and it can describe the delight that thing gives to the person who enjoys it. Scripture uses the word only thirteen times, all in poetry and wisdom writing. It describes friendship, music, married love, wisdom, the unity of God's people, and…

h5274.sum: The Hebrew verb nâʻal means to fasten something securely. In some passages it describes sliding a bar across a door to lock it. In others it describes tying sandals onto someone's feet. Both are acts of fastening, and the word appears only eight times in the Old Testament. Its few uses are vivid. Ehud locks a king's doors behind him. Amnon has a door bolted against his wounded sister Tamar. The bridegroom in the…

h5276.sum: The Hebrew verb nâʻêm means to be pleasant . It describes something sweet, delightful, or beautiful to the person who experiences it. The NKJV usually translates it "pleasant," and also uses "sweet," "delight," and "beauty." The word appears only eight times, yet those few uses cover a wide range of experience. It describes a good piece of land, the friendship between David and Jonathan, the love between a bride and…

h5292.sum: Naarah is the name of two unrelated subjects in the Old Testament: a town on the eastern border of Ephraim's territory (Joshua 16:7) and a woman of the tribe of Judah, one of the two wives of Ashhur, "the father of Tekoa" (1 Chronicles 4:5–6). The name matches the ordinary Hebrew word naʻărâh , meaning "girl" or "young woman." Scripture never explains why a woman or a town carried this name, and nothing in the text…

h5305.sum: Naphish was the eleventh-listed of Ishmael's twelve sons. He was a grandson of Abraham through Hagar, and he became the ancestor of an Arab tribe that bore his name. His name probably means "refreshment" or "refreshed," from a Hebrew root meaning "to breathe" or "to refresh oneself." That meaning is likely but not certain. Naphish appears only three times in Scripture. Two of these are genealogies (Genesis 25:15; 1…

h5315.g: anyone, appetite, breath, breathed, corpse, creature, creatures, dead, desire, life, lives, minded, neck, O, own, person, persons, soul, souls
h5315.sum: The Hebrew word nephesh describes a living, breathing creature: the whole person as alive, needy, and vulnerable before God. English Bibles translate it "soul," "life," "person," "creature," "heart," "desire," "appetite," and often just "I" or "myself." When God breathed into the dust in Genesis 2:7, "man became a living being," a living nephesh . Hebrew speaks of a person's hunger, longing, fear, love, and very…

h5317.sum: Nôpheth is a Hebrew word for honey as it flows from the comb, the freshest and richest sweetness an Israelite could taste. It appears only five times in the Old Testament, and every time it appears in poetry. Its rarity matters. Whether it means real honey that a person eats or serves as a figure of speech, the Bible uses it to teach: what is sweeter than the best honey, what only looks like honey, and who can…

h5320.sum: The Naphtuhim were a people descended from Mizraim, the ancestor of Egypt and a son of Ham. They appear only twice in Scripture, in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:13) and in its repetition in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 1:11). Neither passage gives them any action or story, only a name in the family line of Egypt. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It is almost certainly an Egyptian phrase carried into Hebrew. Two…

h5339.sum: The Hebrew word nitstsân means flower or blossom . It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 2:12: "The flowers appear on the earth." In the surrounding verses the beloved calls his bride to come away with him (Song of Solomon 2:10, 13), and the flowers are part of his reason: winter has ended. The blossoms are the first sign the poem names, and it sets them side by side with singing, the…

h5375.g: arises, away, Bear, bear, bearer, Bearing, bearing, bears, bore, borne, bring, carried, carries, Carry, carry, Carrying, carrying, exalt, exalted, exalting, forgave, forgive, forgiven, Forgives, forgiving, had, has, have, itself, Lift, lift, Lifted, lifted, lifts, Pick, picked, raised, receive, rise, support, Take, take, taken, took, up, you, Yourself
h5375.sum: The Hebrew verb nâsâʼ is one of the busiest words in the Old Testament. Its basic meaning is simple: to lift something up, to carry it, or to bear its weight. Brothers load grain onto donkeys with it, Levites carry the Ark of God with it, and a young soldier earns the title "armorbearer" from it. The same everyday verb also describes lifting the eyes in hope, lifting the voice in weeping, and lifting the face toward…

h5390.sum: The Hebrew noun nᵉshîyqâh means kiss . It appears only twice in the Old Testament, both times in the plural, "kisses." Those two uses stand at opposite ends of human relationships. In Proverbs 27:6 the "kisses of an enemy are deceitful." Warmth is used as a disguise. In Song of Solomon 1:2 the bride cries, "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth," longing for the nearness of the one she loves. The same small…

h542.sum: The Hebrew word ʼâmân means a master craftsman: a skilled artisan whose trained hands produce fine, carefully finished work. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:1 (7:2 in Hebrew numbering); STEPBible counts 1 occurrence in 1 verse in the Leningrad text with its Qere readings. There a husband praises his bride's beauty by comparing the curves of her body to jewels, "the work of the hands of a…

h5434.sum: Seba is first a man and then a people. Genesis names him as the first-listed son of Cush, the son of Ham, and his descendants became a nation remembered in Scripture as distant, wealthy, and impressive. The meaning of the name Seba is unknown. It is a foreign proper name carried over into Hebrew, and no reliable derivation has been established. Seba must not be confused with Sheba, a different name belonging to…

h5454.sum: Sabtah was a son of Cush, a grandson of Ham, and a great-grandson of Noah. His name appears only twice in the Bible, both times in family lists: the Table of Nations in Genesis 10:7 and the matching genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1:9, where the NKJV spells it "Sabta." The meaning of the name is uncertain. It has no clear Hebrew root and probably comes from a non-Hebrew language, perhaps South Arabian. Like many names in…

h5455.sum: Sabteca was the fifth-listed son of Cush, the grandson of Ham, and a great-grandson of Noah. His name appears only twice in Scripture, both times in the list of Cush's sons (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9). The NKJV spells it "Sabtechah" in Genesis and "Sabtecha" in Chronicles. The meaning of the name is unknown. Scholars have compared it with the name of a later Cushite ruler of Egypt, Shabataka, but that…

h5469.sum: The Hebrew word çahar means roundness . It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:2, where the NKJV renders it "rounded": "Your navel is a rounded goblet; It lacks no blended beverage." The word paints a picture of a smooth, curved, well-formed bowl, the kind of vessel that holds wine at a celebration. In the Song, that picture becomes a husband's way of praising the beauty of his bride.

h5473.sum: This Hebrew verb means to fence in, hem in, or set something about with a border. It appears only once in the Bible, in the bridegroom's praise of his bride in Song of Solomon 7:2: "Your waist is a heap of wheat Set about with lilies." Because the word has only this one setting, its meaning is learned from the picture it helps paint. A heap of wheat is harvest, food, and life. Lilies are beauty and fragrance. The…

h549.sum: Amana is a northern height in the mountains beyond Israel's border. Scripture connects the name with two related features: a peak in the Anti-Lebanon range, named in Song of Solomon 4:8 beside Senir and Hermon, and the river of Damascus, which flows down from those mountains. The river is named in 2 Kings 5:12 in a marginal reading that Hebrew scribes preserved. The name probably comes from the Hebrew root meaning…

h5513.sum: "Sinite" is the name of an ancient people descended from Canaan, the son of Ham. The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the same short line of a family record: "the Hivite, the Arkite, and the Sinite" (Genesis 10:17; 1 Chronicles 1:15). Scripture tells us nothing about what the Sinites did, whom they fought, or where they worshiped. We know only that they came from Canaan's line and were listed…

h5577.sum: The Hebrew word çançin appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:8, where the NKJV translates it "branches." The word does not describe ordinary limbs or leafy fronds. It describes the fruit-stalks of the date palm, the sturdy stems at the top of the tree that hold the heavy, sweet clusters of dates. The bridegroom has just compared his bride's stature to a palm tree. When he says, "I will go up to the…

h559.g: anyone, boast, called, continually, had, has, people, said, Say, say, Saying, saying, Says, says, someone, speak, spoke, spoken, tell, thought, told, You, you
h559.sum: The Hebrew verb ʼâmar is the Old Testament's ordinary word for saying something. Most often it means simply "said," "say," or "saying," and it carries the conversations of Scripture. Patriarchs bargain, kings give orders, widows plead, and prophets argue with this word. Depending on the setting it can also mean answer, tell, command, promise, or even think, because Hebrew describes thinking as saying in one's heart…

h5601.sum: The Hebrew word çappîyr names a precious deep-blue stone, translated "sapphire" in the NKJV. Many scholars believe the ancient stone was lapis lazuli: an opaque, rich blue stone often flecked with gold, rather than the clear gem sold as sapphire today. Its color matters. Scripture's most important uses of the stone appear where heaven meets the presence of God. At Sinai, the elders of Israel saw beneath God's feet…

h5638.sum: The Hebrew word çᵉthâv means winter . It appears only once in the Bible, in the Song of Solomon's springtime invitation: "For lo, the winter is past, The rain is over and gone" (Song of Solomon 2:11). In ancient Israel, winter was the season of heavy, cold rains rather than snow and ice. Those rains soaked the ground, made travel hard, and kept people indoors. Yet without them there would be no flowers, figs, or…

h5643.sum: The Hebrew word çêther means a cover, a hiding place, or something kept secret. Most often it simply describes something covered or out of sight: a covert in the hills, a private message, a conversation held "secretly." Scripture uses the word in two opposite directions. People use a çêther to hide sin, such as idols set up "in secret," adultery under a disguise, or slander whispered behind a neighbor's back. God,…

h567.sum: The Amorites were one of the peoples living in Canaan before Israel entered the land. Genesis lists them among the descendants of Canaan, and the Old Testament remembers them for their powerful kingdoms, especially those of Sihon and Og east of the Jordan and the five-king alliance Joshua defeated in the south. Sometimes "Amorite" names a specific people or kingdom. At other times it stands for all the inhabitants…

h5677.sum: Eber is best known as the descendant of Shem through whom the Bible traces the line that leads to Abraham. Genesis lists him as the son of Salah (spelled Shelah in Chronicles and Luke), the great-grandson of Shem, and the father of Peleg and Joktan (Genesis 10:21–25; 11:14–17). The name is generally understood to mean "beyond" or "the region beyond." It comes from a Hebrew word family built on a verb meaning "to…

h5739.sum: The Hebrew word ʻêder means a flock or herd: a gathered group of animals, usually sheep or goats, moving and grazing together under someone's care. In Genesis it counts Jacob's wealth and names the "droves" he sent ahead to Esau. In Proverbs it calls for careful stewardship. In the Song of Solomon it pictures a bride's beauty. In the prophets it becomes the name of Israel itself: "the LORD's flock" (Jeremiah 13:17).

h5762.sum: Avith was a city in the land of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. It appears only twice in Scripture, both times as "his city" of Hadad the son of Bedad, one of the early kings who "reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the children of Israel" (Genesis 36:31, 35; 1 Chronicles 1:46). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Strong's and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the gloss "ruins," and older…

h5780.sum: Uz is the name of three men in the biblical genealogies and of a land east of Israel. The land is by far the most important. The first is a grandson of Shem through Aram (Genesis 10:23; 1 Chronicles 1:17). The second is the firstborn son of Abraham's brother Nahor (Genesis 22:21). The third is a son of Dishan, one of the Horite clan chiefs of Seir, later the territory of Edom (Genesis 36:28; 1 Chronicles 1:42). The…

h5782.g: Awake, awake, awaken, had, has, himself, myself, roused, Stir, stir, stirred, stirring, stirs, up
h5782.sum: The Hebrew verb ʻûwr means to wake up, to rouse, or to stir into action. It describes a sleeper coming awake, a warrior springing into battle, a love that should not be stirred before its time, and an eagle stirring its nest. Behind its many uses lies one idea: something at rest, dormant, or idle is roused and set in motion.

h5794.sum: The Hebrew word ʻaz describes force that is hard to resist. It can mean a strong people or a fortified border, a strong east wind, deep waters, or a lion. It can also describe something harsh in a person: fierce anger, a hard face, a rough answer, an appetite that never has enough. The word itself does not decide whether that strength is good or evil. Everything depends on who holds it and how it is used.

h5795.sum: The Hebrew word ʻêz means goat . It refers to the ordinary goat of Israel's flocks, often the female, and sometimes the whole herd. Goats gave milk, meat, and hair for weaving. Because they were so common and so useful, the word appears wherever Israel's daily life appears: in a family's wealth, a gift, a meal for a guest, and a household's supply of milk.

h583.sum: Enosh was the son of Seth and the grandson of Adam and Eve. He belongs to the third generation of the human story, before the flood. His name is the ordinary Hebrew word for "man," a word that often stresses human frailty and mortality, so it is usually understood as "mortal man." The connection to a root meaning "to be weak" is commonly proposed, though it is less certain than the plain sense "man." Genesis records…

h5844.g: cover, covered, covers, himself, veils, Yourself
h5844.sum: The Hebrew verb ʻâṭâh means to wrap, cover, or clothe, usually by drawing something around oneself like a cloak. Sometimes the covering is literal. Samuel appears "covered with a mantle," and a woman veils herself among the shepherds. Most of the time, though, Scripture uses the word as a picture. A person or thing becomes so fully surrounded by a condition that it serves as a garment, and everyone who looks can see…

h5849.sum: The Hebrew verb ʻâṭar means to encircle or surround, and from that picture it came to mean to crown . A crown is a band that circles the head, so the same word can describe an army closing a ring around its target or a king receiving a wreath of honor. The word appears only seven times in the Old Testament, and nearly every use is striking. Saul's soldiers are "encircling" David to capture him, while David sings…

h5850.sum: The Hebrew word ʻăṭârâh means a crown: the gold circlet of a king, the festive wreath of a celebration, or anything that serves as a person's visible honor. In Scripture it sits on the heads of conquering kings, bridegrooms, and rescued men like Mordecai. It also moves beyond literal headgear. Proverbs calls a good wife, gray hair, and grandchildren a crown. The prophets warn that a proud nation's crown will fall…

h5858.sum: Ebal is best known as Mount Ebal, the mountain facing Mount Gerizim across the valley at Shechem in the heart of the Promised Land. Moses commanded that when Israel entered Canaan, the curse of God's law would be set on Ebal and the blessing on Gerizim. On Ebal Israel was also to raise great plastered stones inscribed with the law and build an altar of uncut stones for burnt offerings and peace offerings. Joshua…

h5867.sum: Elam is the name of an ancient nation east of Babylon. It is also the name of several Israelites who had no connection to that nation. In Genesis, Elam is a son of Shem and the ancestor of a people who lived beyond the Tigris River in the highlands of what is now southwestern Iran, with Susa (Shushan) as their great city. The name is commonly explained as "highland," associated with the Mesopotamian name for the…

h5891.sum: Ephah is a name carried by three different people in the Old Testament. The best known is Ephah the son of Midian, a grandson of Abraham through Keturah, whose descendants became an Arabian tribe also called Ephah (Genesis 25:4; 1 Chronicles 1:33; Isaiah 60:6). The other two belong to the tribe of Judah: a woman named Ephah who was the concubine of Caleb and bore him three sons (1 Chronicles 2:46), and a man named…

h5892.g: anguish, Cities, cities, City, city, city’s, Ir, O, own
h5892.sum: The Hebrew word ʻîyr is the Old Testament's ordinary word for a city or town. It can name a great walled capital like Jerusalem, a small country town, or a modest outpost. Sometimes it stands for the people who live there. In most uses, an ʻîyr is a gathered and defended community: people living together, usually behind walls and gates, and looking to those defenses for safety.

h5902.sum: Iram was one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother. His name appears only twice in Scripture, as the last entry in the list of Edom's chiefs (Genesis 36:43; 1 Chronicles 1:54). The meaning of the name is probable rather than certain. It seems to come from the Hebrew word for "city" or "town," and lexicons suggest a sense such as "belonging to a city" or "citizen." Genesis lists…

h5907.sum: Achbor is the name of two men in the Old Testament. The first is an Edomite remembered only as the father of Baal-Hanan, one of the early kings of Edom who reigned before Israel had a king (Genesis 36:38–39; 1 Chronicles 1:49). The second, and far more significant, is Achbor the son of Michaiah, a trusted official of King Josiah of Judah. When the Book of the Law was found in the temple, Josiah sent Achbor with four…

h5933.sum: Alvah was one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother. He appears only in the list of Edomite clan leaders in Genesis 36:40 and in the Chronicler's repetition of that list, where the name is spelled "Aliah" (1 Chronicles 1:51). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Some connect it with a root that suggests height or loftiness (as Hitchcock's dictionary does), while Strong's and…

h5935.sum: Alvan was a son of Shobal, one of the Horite chiefs who lived in Mount Seir before Esau's descendants took over the region. He appears only in the two parallel lists of Seir's family. Genesis 36:23 spells his name Alvan, and 1 Chronicles 1:40 spells it Alian. The difference is often explained as a variation between two similar Hebrew letters. The meaning of the name is uncertain. If it comes from a Hebrew root…

h5959.sum: The Hebrew word ʻalmâh means a young woman or maiden. The NKJV translates it "virgin" or "maiden." The Old Testament uses the word only seven times. In ancient Israel a young woman who had not yet married was customarily expected to be a virgin, and that association stands behind the NKJV's "virgin." The word itself, though, focuses on her youth and stage of life. What each passage says about a particular woman,…

h5968.sum: The Hebrew verb ʻâlaph means to wrap or cover something completely. It appears only five times in the Old Testament, and it moves in two directions. In Genesis, Tamar wraps herself in a veil, and in the Song of Solomon the beloved's body is "inlaid with sapphires," covered with jewels. In three prophetic passages, the same word describes people who faint, overcome by weakness as though something has closed over them.

h5978.sum: ʻImmâd is a Hebrew preposition meaning "with," closely related to the much more common ʻim. It carries the ending "me" (ʻimmâdî, "with me"). Context decides what being "with me" means. It can describe a person standing beside the speaker, an action aimed at the speaker for good or harm, something the speaker carries inwardly, or something that belongs to the speaker. With the prefix "from," it marks movement away…

h5982.sum: The Hebrew word ʻammûwd means a pillar or column: something that stands upright and bears weight. Scripture uses it for the posts of the tabernacle and its court, the great bronze pillars at the entrance of Solomon's temple, and the columns of palaces and pagan temples. It also uses it for the column of cloud by day and fire by night in which the LORD led Israel through the wilderness. Poets use the same word for…

h6002.sum: Amalek is first the name of a grandson of Esau, born to Eliphaz by his concubine Timna (Genesis 36:12), and then, far more often, the name of the desert people descended from him. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Proposed derivations exist, but none is established, and Scripture itself never builds on the name's meaning. The Amalekites lived as nomads and raiders in the Negev and Sinai regions south of Canaan.…

h6010.sum: The Hebrew word ʻêmeq means a valley in the sense of a broad, open lowland. It describes the wide, fairly flat land between ranges of hills, where farmers grew grain and armies could gather in great numbers. In Scripture these valleys are where harvests ripen and where kings meet. They are also where Israel faced some of its most frightening enemies: iron chariots in the plains, the Midianite horde in Jezreel, and…

h6034.sum: Anah is the name of two closely related men among the Horites, the people who lived in the mountains of Seir, south of the Dead Sea, before Esau's descendants took the land. The first Anah was a son of Seir the Horite and one of the chiefs of his people (Genesis 36:20, 29). The second was his nephew, a son of Zibeon (Genesis 36:24). This younger Anah became the father of Aholibamah, one of Esau's wives, and of a son…

h6047.sum: The Anamim were an ancient people descended from Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt, who was a son of Ham and a grandson of Noah. Their name appears only twice in the Bible. Both times it comes in the same line of the same genealogy: "Mizraim begot Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim" (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). Scripture tells us nothing else about them. We do not know where they lived with any certainty,…

h6081.sum: Epher is the name of three different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused. The first is a son of Midian and a grandson of Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:4; 1 Chronicles 1:33). The second is a man of Judah, listed as a son of Ezrah (1 Chronicles 4:17). The third is a clan leader in the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan, remembered as one of the "mighty men of valor, famous men" (1…

h6082.sum: The Hebrew word ʻôpher means a fawn, the young of a deer or gazelle. It appears only five times in the Bible, and every use is in the Song of Solomon, where it serves as a picture of love. Three times the bride uses it for her beloved. She calls him "a young stag" who comes leaping over the mountains and whom she urges to hurry back to her. Twice the bridegroom uses it for the bride, comparing her beauty to "two…

h6119.sum: The Hebrew word ʻâqêb means heel . It names the back of the human foot or the hoof of an animal. Because the heel is the part of us that touches the ground and trails behind, the word also came to mean footsteps (the tracks a person leaves and the path a person walks) and the rear of something. The NKJV translates it as heel, footsteps, steps, hooves, rear guard, and "at last."

h6156.sum: The Hebrew adjective ʻârêb means sweet , pleasant or delightful . It describes something that is a pleasure to experience. It is not the usual word for the taste of sugar or honey. Hebrew normally uses another word for that kind of sweetness. ʻârêb names the satisfaction a person feels in something, and because it describes that felt pleasure, the word is neither good nor evil in itself. Everything depends on what…

h6170.sum: The Hebrew word ʻărûwgâh names a prepared planting bed: a raised or terraced plot of ground that someone has marked out, worked, planted, and tended. It appears only four times in the Old Testament, twice in the Song of Solomon and twice in Ezekiel. Those two settings could hardly be more different. In the Song, the bride compares her beloved's face to "a bed of spices" (5:13), and she says he has gone to "the beds…

h6186.g: against, arrange, compare, formation, Order, order, taxed
h6186.w: Arrange, Set In Order, Array, Prepare
h6186.sum: The Hebrew verb ʻârak means to set things in a row: to arrange, lay out, or put in order. Scripture uses it when Abraham lays the wood on the altar, when priests set out the showbread and tend the lamps, and when armies draw up their battle lines. It is also used for laying out a legal case, preparing a table for a meal, and placing two things side by side to compare them or set a price. The common thread is…

h6208.sum: "Arkite" is the name of an ancient people descended from Canaan, the son of Ham. The Bible uses the word only twice, both times in the same short line of a family record: "the Hivite, the Arkite, and the Sinite" (Genesis 10:17; 1 Chronicles 1:15). The Arkites are linked with the old coastal city of Arqa in what is now northern Lebanon. Ancient records outside the Bible know this city as Irqata. The name places…

h6210.sum: The Hebrew word ʻeres simply means a bed or couch: the frame or furnished piece of furniture where a person sleeps, rests, recovers from sickness, or reclines at ease. The NKJV renders it "bed," "couch," and "bedstead." It is not a common word, but Scripture places it where people are least guarded. There is the giant king's iron bed, the sufferer's sleepless bed, the sick man's bed, the seductress's perfumed bed,…

h6213.g: acquired, act, acted, acts, appointed, been, celebrate, certainly, Deal, deal, dealt, did, Do, do, does, doing, done, Execute, execute, had, has, Have, have, Made, made, Make, make, Maker, maker, makes, making, may, Observe, observe, observed, observing, offer, offered, prepare, prepared, show, used, work, worker, works, You, you
h6213.sum: The Hebrew verb ʻâsâh is the Old Testament's everyday word for action. It means to do, make, perform, prepare, or produce, and English translations render it in dozens of ways: "made," "did," "done," "show," "deal," "keep," "execute," "yield." God uses it when He makes the sky and the stars. A cook uses it when preparing a meal, a craftsman when building an altar, a nation when committing a sin, and a tree when…

h6215.sum: Esau was the firstborn twin son of Isaac and Rebekah, the older brother of Jacob, and the ancestor of the Edomites who settled in the mountain country of Seir. Genesis ties his name to his appearance at birth: "the first came out red. He was like a hairy garment all over; so they called his name Esau" (Genesis 25:25). The name is therefore usually understood as "hairy" or "rough." That meaning rests on the wordplay…

h6227.sum: The Hebrew word ʻâshân simply means "smoke," the dark, rising cloud given off by fire. Scripture uses it for ordinary things such as a chimney, a burning city, or a stinging irritant in the eyes. The biblical writers also notice what smoke does. It rises high and can be seen from far away. It hides what is behind it. Then it thins out and disappears. Each of these qualities becomes a way of teaching about God and…

h6247.sum: The Hebrew word ʻesheth appears only once in the Bible, in the bride's praise of her beloved in Song of Solomon 5:14: "His body is carved ivory inlaid with sapphires." It describes a worked slab or plate of solid material with a smooth, finished surface. The NKJV translates it "carved," which emphasizes skilled workmanship. Other translations say "bright" or "polished," which emphasize the gleam of the finished…

h6258.sum: ʻAttâh is the ordinary Hebrew word for "now." It points to the present moment in contrast to what came before or what lies ahead. Very often, especially in the phrases "and now" or "now therefore," it does more than tell time. It works as a hinge in speech, moving from what has been said to what must happen because of it. A speaker reviews history, states a grievance, or recalls a promise, and then ʻattâh turns the…

h6291.sum: The Hebrew word pag means the green, early figs that start to form on a fig tree at the turn from winter to spring, well before the main summer harvest. It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 2:13, where the beloved calls the woman he loves out into a world coming back to life: "The fig tree puts forth her green figs, And the vines with the tender grapes Give a good smell. Rise up, my love, my fair…

h631.g: Bind, bind, Binding, binds, bound, girded, Harness, prisoners
h631.sum: The Hebrew verb ʼâçar means to bind . Scripture uses it for the ropes Samson's enemies tied around him, the bronze fetters placed on Judah's last kings, and the cell where Joseph was "confined." The same verb also describes hitching animals to a cart or chariot so they are ready for a task. Most strikingly, it describes a person "binding" his own soul with a vow before the Lord. In each case, something is fastened…

h6310.g: According, according, edge, mouth, mouths, own, word
h6310.sum: The Hebrew word peh means mouth . It is the ordinary word for the mouth a person eats and speaks with. The same word names the opening of a well or a sack, the "edge" of a sword, and the spoken word or command that comes from someone's mouth. When the NKJV says Israel moved "at the command of the LORD," the Hebrew says they moved at the mouth of the LORD. When Joshua strikes a city "with the edge of the sword," the…

h6315.sum: The Hebrew verb pûwach means to breathe or to blow . It describes breath or wind moving outward, and Scripture uses that picture in several ways. Wind blows across a garden. The day breathes as the cool breeze rises. An arrogant man puffs at his enemies. A needy person yearns for safety. Scoffers blow on a city until it bursts into flame. Most often, in Proverbs, the word describes a witness who utters lies or,…

h6316.sum: Put is the name of the third son of Ham listed in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:6), and of the African people descended from him. The meaning of the name is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary proposes a link to an old word for "bow," but the evidence is thin, and Scripture itself never builds anything on the name. English readers can easily miss Put because the NKJV keeps the name "Put" in Genesis, 1 Chronicles,…

h6337.sum: The Hebrew word pâz means pure or fine gold, gold valued for its purity and worth. It is a rare word, used only nine times, and always in poetry or prophecy. It never appears in a merchant's ledger or a building list. Scripture uses it as the highest measure of earthly value and then sets something above it. The psalmist says God's judgments are "more to be desired" than "much fine gold" (Psalm 19:10), and he…

h6343.sum: Pachad is a Hebrew word for dread. It names the shaking, heart-stopping fear that grips a person when danger, judgment, or the presence of God suddenly becomes real. The NKJV usually translates it "fear," "dread," or "terror." Scripture uses it for the panic that falls on enemy nations, the night fears that trouble the vulnerable, the private anguish of a suffering man like Job, and the terror of proud people when…

h6370.sum: The Hebrew word pîylegesh means a concubine: a woman joined to a man as a secondary wife. She was publicly recognized as belonging to his household and was expected to be faithful to him, but she held lower standing than a primary wife. Scripture does not set out one uniform package of rights for her across every period, and her children did not necessarily share the chief inheritance, as when Abraham gave gifts to…

h6373.sum: Pinon is one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother. The name appears only twice, in the closing list of Edomite chiefs in Genesis 36:41 and in the parallel record in 1 Chronicles 1:52. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It is widely thought to share a root with Punon, a place in the Arabah where Israel camped during the wilderness years, but no meaning has been firmly…

h6385.sum: The Hebrew verb pâlag means "to divide" or "to split," in the sense of cutting something apart or cutting a channel through it. It appears only four times in the Old Testament, and in each use God is, or is most naturally understood to be, the one who divides. Genesis and 1 Chronicles use it to explain the name of Peleg, "for in his days the earth was divided." The surrounding chapters make it a well-supported…

h6389.sum: Peleg was a descendant of Shem who lived after the Flood. He was the son of Eber, the brother of Joktan, and the father of Reu, and he stands in the family line that runs from Noah to Abraham. His name means "division." Genesis explains why he was given it: "for in his days the earth was divided" (Genesis 10:25). Scripture records no words or deeds of Peleg. What it does preserve is his name, his family, and his…

h639.g: anger, double, face, faces, nose, Noses, nostrils
h639.sum: The Hebrew word ʼaph begins with the human nose: the nostrils that draw breath, the face pressed to the ground in a bow. From there it became the Old Testament's most common word for anger. The connection comes from ordinary experience. An angry person breathes hard, the nostrils flare, and the face flushes. Scripture uses this vivid, physical word for human temper and for the holy anger of God. It does not treat…

h6400.sum: The Hebrew word pelach means a piece or slice of something larger. Scripture uses it for two very different things: the heavy stones of a household hand-mill, and a slice of fruit or fig cake. It appears only six times, yet those few uses move from violent judgment to tender mercy to the language of love.

h6430.sum: Pᵉlishtîy is the Hebrew word for a Philistine, a member of the people who lived along the southern coast of Canaan in cities such as Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, and Gath. The NKJV usually renders it "Philistines" for the nation, "the Philistine" for an individual such as Goliath, and occasionally "Philistia" for their land. The word names a people. It does not mean "enemy" or "wicked." Still, no nation pressed harder…

h6435.sum: Pên introduces an outcome that someone wants to prevent. It usually follows a command, a warning, a decision, or a prayer, and then names the danger that the command, warning, decision, or prayer is meant to avoid. The NKJV most often renders it "lest." After words like "beware" or "swear," it often becomes a simple "not," and in Genesis 31:31 it appears as "Perhaps," voicing Jacob's fear. Wherever it appears, pên…

h6437.g: back, Corner, face, faces, have, Turn, turn, turned, turns
h6437.sum: The Hebrew verb pânâh means to turn: to face a direction, turn toward someone, turn away from something, or turn obstacles aside. The word is closely related to the Hebrew word for "face," so the verb describes directing your face somewhere. For this reason the NKJV can render it "turn," "look," "regard," "respect," "face," and even "prepare." Moses looks this way and that before striking the Egyptian. Ezekiel's…

h6440.g: Because, because, Before, before, face, faced, faces, Facing, facing, forward, front, person, Presence, presence, surface
h6440.sum: The Hebrew word pânîym means "face." Because the face is where a person is recognized, where feelings show, and where one person meets another, the word naturally came to mean "presence." To be before someone's face was to be in their company and under their gaze. The same word also became Hebrew's most common way of saying "before," "in front of," "from," and even "because of." It can describe the surface of the…

h6464.sum: Pau was a royal city in Edom, the land of Esau's descendants south and southeast of the Dead Sea. Scripture names it only as the city of Hadar, the eighth and last-listed of the Edomite kings in Genesis 36. First Chronicles 1:50 repeats the record, calling the king Hadad and the city Pai. No one knows exactly what the name means. It is often linked to a Hebrew root meaning "to cry out" or "to bleat," but that…

h6481.sum: The Hebrew verb pâtsaʻ means to wound, bruise, or crush. It describes a real blow that breaks or injures the body. The word appears only three times in the Old Testament, once in each major part of the Hebrew Bible. In Deuteronomy 23:1 it describes a man injured so that he cannot father children, and that injury keeps him out of "the assembly of the LORD." In 1 Kings 20:37 a prophet asks to be struck so that the…

h650.sum: The Hebrew word ʼâphîyq names a channel: the bed that holds water, especially the deep-cut streambed of a wadi that runs dry in summer and floods after the rains. The NKJV translates it "channels," "streams," "brooks," "rivers," "ravines," "riverbeds," and "valleys." In a few poetic passages in Job, a related sense of something firm or tightly held appears as "beams," "scales," and "mighty." The word describes the…

h6524.g: break, breaking, breaks, broken, bud, budded, flourish, up
h6524.sum: The Hebrew verb pârach describes something breaking forth into view. It is used for a vine bursting into bud, a dead staff sprouting almonds overnight, a desert covered in flowers, and the righteous flourishing like a palm tree. The same word also describes boils breaking out on the skin in Egypt and disease spreading in the laws of Leviticus. The word tells us that something has become visible. The context tells us…

h6529.sum: The Hebrew word pᵉrîy is the Old Testament's ordinary word for fruit: the yield of trees and the produce of fields. It is also used for offspring, both the young of flocks and herds and human children. Scripture speaks of "the fruit of the womb," meaning children, and "the fruit of their thoughts," meaning the outcome of a life. In many uses, fruit is the visible result of something hidden, such as a root, a womb, a…

h6584.g: have, made, off, raid, raided, skin, skinned, Strip, strip, stripped, take, taken
h6584.sum: The Hebrew verb pâshaṭ means to strip something of its covering. It can describe taking off a garment, skinning an animal, stripping armor from a fallen soldier, or soldiers rushing upon a city or a territory in attack, a raid that could end with goods and people carried off. The word itself is morally neutral. Its significance depends on who is doing the stripping, who or what is being stripped, and why. Jonathan…

h6625.sum: Pathrusim is the name of a people. It refers to the descendants of Mizraim (Egypt) who settled in Pathros, the southern stretch of the Nile valley usually called Upper Egypt. The word appears only twice in the Bible. Both times it sits in a list of nations descended from Ham: Genesis 10:14 and its parallel in 1 Chronicles 1:12. Neither verse tells a story about the Pathrusim. They are named, placed in their family…

h6629.sum: The Hebrew word tson names the flock: the sheep and goats that grazed together across the hills of Israel. Abraham's wealth was counted in flocks, and Jacob's family lived by them. Abel offered from his flock, and the Passover lamb came from it. Much of the tabernacle's worship drew on it. The flock was a family's living, its measure of God's blessing, and the animals it brought to worship.

h6634.sum: Tsᵉbâʼ is an Aramaic verb that means to will, choose, or wish. It describes someone wanting an outcome and deciding on it. The word appears only in the Aramaic chapters of Daniel, and nearly every use sits inside one argument. That argument concerns whose will actually governs the world. The NKJV translates it "will," "chooses," and "wished," so English readers easily miss that one word ties these passages together.

h6643.sum: The Hebrew word tsᵉbîy has two faces in the Old Testament. In some passages it means the gazelle, the swift, graceful animal of Israel's hills. In others it means splendor or glory: beauty that stands out and draws the eye. The gazelle appears in Israel's food laws, in descriptions of fast warriors, in a warning to escape a trap, and in the Song of Solomon, where the beloved comes "leaping upon the mountains." The…

h6646.sum: The Hebrew word tsᵉbîyâh means gazelle , and specifically a female gazelle. The gazelle is a slender, swift wild animal of Israel's hill country. This word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the Song of Solomon and both times in the same phrase. The bridegroom tells his bride that her breasts are "like two fawns, twins of a gazelle" (Song of Solomon 4:5; 7:3). The picture is gentle. Twin fawns are soft,…

h6649.sum: Zibeon was a Horite chief who lived in Mount Seir, the rugged highlands south of the Dead Sea that later became the land of Edom. He was one of the sons of Seir the Horite, the clan leaders who held the land before Esau's descendants took it over (Genesis 36:20, 29). His family joined Esau's when Esau married Aholibamah, a descendant of Zibeon usually traced through his son Anah (Genesis 36:2, 14, 24–25), though…

h6664.sum: Tsedeq is the Hebrew word for what is right, meaning what measures up to a true standard. Its roots in Scripture are concrete. The law uses it for honest scales and full weights in the marketplace and for fair verdicts in court. From there the word rises to describe God Himself: His throne rests on righteousness, His Word is righteous through and through, and His judgments never tilt toward the powerful or the bribe.

h6677.sum: The Hebrew word tsavvâʼr means the neck, especially the back of the neck where a yoke sits, a chain hangs, or a weeping brother lays his face. It is an ordinary body word, but Scripture places some of its most important scenes there. Esau embraces Jacob and falls on his neck, Joseph and Benjamin weep on one another's necks, and Joseph falls on the neck of his father Jacob. Jeremiah walks through Jerusalem wearing a…

h668.sum: The Hebrew word ʼappiryôwn means a palanquin, a royal carriage carried on the shoulders of attendants. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 3:9: "Of the wood of Lebanon Solomon the King Made himself a palanquin." The word does not describe a war chariot. It describes a vehicle of peace, honor, and celebration that carries the king on the day of his wedding. Count source — Leningrad Hebrew text…

h6692.sum: The Hebrew verb tsûwts means to blossom or to flourish . In one verse it is translated "gazing." Most of its uses picture a plant bursting into flower. Scripture uses that moment of bloom to tell two very different stories. Grass flourishes in the morning and withers by evening, and so does human life (Psalm 90:6; Psalm 103:15). The wicked flourish too, but only "that they may be destroyed forever" (Psalm 92:7). As…

h6696.g: besieged, Bind, binds, bound, distress, distressed, fashioned, hindered, lay, narrow, siege, up, wrapped
h6696.sum: The Hebrew verb tsûwr is used for several actions that close something in or give it form: surrounding a city, tying something up, and shaping metal. Most often it is a word of war. Armies "besiege" cities, surrounding them until food runs out and the gates open. The same word also describes tying silver into bags, casting bronze in a mold, and fashioning gold into an idol. Everything depends on who is doing the…

h6703.sum: The Hebrew word tsach describes something glaring, bright, and unclouded. It names the kind of intensity nothing softens: a complexion that shines, a summer heat with no cloud to filter it, a wilderness wind with no moisture in it, and speech that comes out clear instead of stumbling. The NKJV renders it four different ways in its only four occurrences: "white," "clear," "plainly," and "dry." Behind each English…

h6721.sum: Sidon was an ancient Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast, north of Israel. Genesis also gives the name to a person: "Canaan begot Sidon his firstborn" (Genesis 10:15). The firstborn of Canaan and the old coastal city stand at the head of the Canaanite peoples. The name most likely means "hunting" or "fishing." It is usually traced to a Hebrew root meaning to hunt or catch, which suits a seafaring town,…

h6738.sum: The Hebrew word tsêl means shadow or shade , the cool patch of ground where something stands between a person and the sun. In the hot, dry lands of the Bible, shade was a matter of survival. Scripture uses the word for the shade of trees, a booth, and a great rock, and for the moving shadow on Hezekiah's sundial. It also uses the word as a picture of protection. A king, an empire, an ally, money, and wisdom can each…

h6757.sum: Tsalmâveth is the Hebrew Bible's word for the deepest darkness a person can know. The NKJV renders it "shadow of death" every time it appears. Its range covers the grave, a killing wilderness, the black interior of a mine, the gloom over a grieving face, and the darkness of people imprisoned by their own rebellion. It names more than the moment of dying. It describes the darkness in which death feels near,…

h6777.sum: The Hebrew word tsammâh means a woman's veil, a covering over the face or head. It appears only four times in the Old Testament, and those few uses fall on opposite sides of a sharp line. Three times in the Song of Solomon, the bridegroom praises his bride's eyes and temples as he sees them "behind your veil." Her veil is part of her beauty. It keeps her loveliness reserved, while the one who loves her still sees it…

h6786.sum: "Zemarite" is the name of an ancient people descended from Canaan, the son of Ham. It appears only twice in Scripture, both times in the same short line of a genealogy: "the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite" (Genesis 10:18; 1 Chronicles 1:16). The word carries no abstract meaning. It names a real tribe, usually linked with the coastal city of Sumur (Simyra) in what is now coastal Syria, near the far…
