h6825.sum: Zepho was a grandson of Esau, the son of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn by Adah (Genesis 36:10–11). Zepho's own mother is not identified. He appears only in the family records of Edom. Genesis lists him among Eliphaz's sons and then names him "Chief Zepho," one of the clan leaders who governed Esau's descendants in the land of Seir (Genesis 36:15). First Chronicles repeats his name in its survey of the nations…

h6828.sum: The Hebrew word tsâphôwn simply means north . Most often it marks a direction: a border running northward, the table set on the north side of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:35), a gate facing north in Ezekiel's temple. Because Israel's great enemies, Assyria and Babylon, usually came down on the land from the north, the prophets turned this ordinary compass word into a word heavy with warning. Jeremiah saw calamity…

h687.sum: Ezer was a Horite chief in the land of Seir, the rugged mountain country south of the Dead Sea that later became Edom. He was one of the seven sons of Seir the Horite, and he headed a clan whose sons are named as Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan (called Jaakan in Chronicles). His name, ʼEtser, comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to store up" or "lay up," so it is usually understood to mean "treasure" or "store." He should not…

h6887.sum: The Hebrew verb tsârar means to bind, wrap, cramp, or hem in. It can describe something physical: kneading bowls bundled in clothing, a stone tied into a sling, or a place too small to live in. It can also describe a person pressed in by circumstances until no way out remains. That person is in "distress" or "trouble." And it can describe someone who presses others in, the "enemy" or "adversary" who harasses and…

h6929.sum: Kedemah is the last-named of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. His name appears only twice in Scripture, both times in a list: once in the family record of Ishmael (Genesis 25:15) and again in Chronicles' retelling of the same line (1 Chronicles 1:31). His name is traditionally understood to mean "eastward" or "toward the east." It is related to the Hebrew word for "east," which can also carry the…

h6938.sum: Kedar was the second-listed son of Ishmael and a grandson of Abraham through Hagar (Genesis 25:13; 1 Chronicles 1:29). His descendants became a powerful nomadic Arabian tribe east of Israel. They were known for their archers, their large flocks, and their black tents, and the Bible later uses the name for the people and their desert region. The name is generally traced to a Hebrew root meaning "to be dark" or…

h6965.g: Arise, arise, arisen, arises, arose, confirm, confirmed, endure, Establish, establish, established, Get, has, have, imposed, make, may, out, raise, raised, raises, Rise, rise, risen, rises, rose, rouse, set, stand, stands, stood, Strengthen, up
h6965.sum: This Hebrew verb means to rise, stand up, or arise. Most of the time it describes ordinary movement: getting out of bed, standing to greet a guest, or rising to set out on a journey. It can also mean to stand firm or hold good, as when God declares that His counsel "shall stand," that is, it will endure and not be overturned. When the verb is used to mean make something stand , it can mean to raise up, set up,…

h6967.sum: The Hebrew word qôwmâh means height. It can describe how tall a building or object is, how tall a person stands, or how high a tree grows. Most of its uses are plain measurements: the height of Noah's ark, the ark of the testimony, the altars, Solomon's temple, and its bronze pillars. In many of these passages God is the one who sets the measurements. People do not design their own way into His presence. He gives…

h6977.sum: The Hebrew word qᵉvutstsâh means locks of hair: the curls or tresses of a person's head. It appears only twice in the Bible, both times in Song of Solomon 5, and both times it describes the hair of the bride's beloved. That rarity matters. The same small, physical detail appears at two very different moments in the bride's story, and the contrast between those moments is where the word's significance lies.

h6982.sum: The Hebrew word qôwrâh means a beam: a heavy timber cut and set in place to span the walls of a building and hold up its roof. It appears only five times in the Old Testament. Because there are so few uses, each one stands out. The sons of the prophets haul beams from the Jordan to build a place to live. Solomon covers the beams of the Temple with gold. The Song of Solomon describes the lovers' shelter: "The beams…

h6989.sum: Keturah was a woman Abraham married. Genesis introduces her after the narrative of Sarah's death and Isaac's marriage, and on the traditional sequential reading the marriage came late in Abraham's life. Genesis introduces her in one plain line: "Abraham again took a wife, and her name was Keturah" (Genesis 25:1). Her name is widely understood to come from the Hebrew root associated with incense and the rising smoke…

h6996.sum: The Hebrew word qâṭân means small . It can describe a small cloud or a lighter weight, a younger son or the youngest daughter, or a person and family that count for little in the eyes of others. The NKJV translates it as "small," "little," "younger," "youngest," and "least." Its natural opposite is gâdôl , great , and the two words often stand side by side.

h6999.g: burn, burned, had, incense, made, Offer, offer, offered, offering, Perfumed
h6999.sum: The Hebrew verb qâṭar means to make something rise as smoke. Usually the smoke is a fragrant offering burned before God. The priests used the word for burning whole burnt offerings, and the fat of other sacrifices, on the bronze altar, and for burning sweet incense on the golden altar every morning and evening. In these settings the fire does more than destroy. It sends the offering upward to God as something He…

h7018.sum: Kenan was one of the early patriarchs before the flood. He was the son of Enosh, the father of Mahalalel, and the fourth generation from Adam through Seth. Readers of the NKJV will find him under the spelling "Cainan" in Genesis 5:9–14 and 1 Chronicles 1:2, and again in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:37). The meaning of his name is uncertain. Scholars have connected it with a Hebrew root meaning "to acquire" or…

h7068.sum: The Hebrew word qinʼâh names a burning, consuming passion that will not rest while something it cares about is threatened. The NKJV translates it as "jealousy," "zeal," or "envy," and the English word changes because the heart behind the passion changes. In a husband who fears his marriage is being betrayed, it is jealousy. In the LORD, it is the fierce love that will not share His people with idols and the tireless…

h7070.g: branches, Calamus, cane, reed, reeds, rod, rods, scales, shaft, stalk
h7070.sum: The Hebrew word qâneh means a reed or stalk: the tall, hollow, jointed plant that grows by water. The same word names a stalk of grain and the fragrant "sweet cane" used in the holy anointing oil. Because a reed is long, straight, and segmented, it also names things with that shape, such as the beam of a merchant's scales and the measuring rod an angelic surveyor carried through Ezekiel's visionary temple. In…

h7073.sum: Kenaz is the name of several men in the Old Testament. The first is an Edomite chief, a grandson of Esau through his son Eliphaz (Genesis 36:11, 15). The most significant is a man of Judah remembered as the father of Othniel, the first judge of Israel (Joshua 15:17; Judges 3:9). A third is a later descendant of Caleb, the son of Elah (1 Chronicles 4:15). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Strong's suggests a…

h7076.sum: The Hebrew word qinnâmôwn means cinnamon, the fragrant inner bark of a tree that did not grow in Israel. It had to come by long trade routes, which made it rare and very expensive. The Old Testament names it only three times, and each use places this costly fragrance in a very different setting. In Exodus 30 God commands that cinnamon be blended into the holy anointing oil that set apart the tabernacle and its…

h7092.sum: The Hebrew verb qâphats describes drawing something together or closing it tight. A hand can close around what it holds, and a mouth can clamp shut. In one poetic verse the word means to leap or skip instead. The NKJV translates the word as "shut," "stops," "taken out of the way," and once as "skipping." The Old Testament uses it only seven times, so each use carries weight. Deuteronomy forbids God's people to shut…

h7094.sum: The Hebrew verb qâtsab means to cut off or to shear. It names a plain, physical action: cutting or clipping something off. It appears only twice in the Old Testament, and both uses are memorable. In 2 Kings 6:6, the prophet Elisha "cut off a stick" and threw it into the Jordan River, and the lost iron ax head floated to the surface. In Song of Solomon 4:2, the bridegroom compares his bride's teeth to "a flock of…

h713.sum: The Hebrew word ʼargâmân means "purple." It names the costly reddish-purple dye of the ancient world and the wool or thread colored with it. The dye came from sea snails and was gathered in tiny amounts, so purple cloth was rare and expensive. It became the recognized color of kings, high officials, and great wealth.

h7141.sum: Korah is the name of several men in the Old Testament. Edom's family records mention one or two Korahs (the references may concern the same chief or clan), and one appears in the genealogy of Judah. The Korah who matters most is the Levite, son of Izhar and grandson of Kohath, who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Numbers 16). The name is traditionally understood to mean "baldness," and some…

h717.sum: The Hebrew verb ʼârâh means to pluck or gather produce from a plant, such as picking fruit from a vine or gathering fragrant myrrh in a garden. The word occurs 2 times in 2 verses of the Hebrew Bible, and the two uses could hardly be further apart. In Psalm 80:12 strangers strip the fruit from Israel's vine after God has broken down its hedges. In Song of Solomon 5:1 the bridegroom enters his own garden and gathers…

h7181.sum: The Hebrew verb qâshab means to listen closely, to pay attention, to give heed. It describes a person deliberately turning ear and mind toward someone who is speaking. The NKJV usually renders it "heed," "listen," "attend," or "give attention." Scripture uses the word in two directions. People are called to listen to God, to His wisdom, and to His prophets. God is asked, and sometimes said, to listen to His people.

h7186.sum: The Hebrew word qâsheh describes something hard: hard to bear, hard to move, or hard to soften. English translations render it many ways, including "hard," "rough," "cruel," "harsh," "stiff," "stubborn," "burdensome," and even "sorrowful." The variety reflects how widely the word is used. It can describe the crushing labor Pharaoh forced on Israel, the rough words of a foolish king, the stiff neck of a people who…

h7200.g: appear, appeared, appears, Behold, certainly, Consider, consider, enjoy, has, Look, look, looked, looking, looks, one, present, presented, saw, See, see, Seeing, seeing, seen, seer, sees, Show, show, showed, shown, shows, You, you
h7200.sum: Râʼâh is the ordinary Hebrew verb "to see," and it fills the Old Testament with eyes that look, notice, examine, and understand. Yet Scripture uses this plain word for some of its most important truths. In Genesis 1, God sees what He has made and judges it good. In the wilderness, Hagar names Him the God who sees her. On Mount Moriah, Abraham says that God will "see to" the lamb, and the NKJV rightly translates it…

h721.sum: "Arvadite" is a Hebrew name for a people: the Arvadites, a Canaanite clan who lived in Arvad, an island city off the northern coast of Phoenicia (modern Arwad, Syria). The word appears only twice in the Bible, in Genesis 10:18 and 1 Chronicles 1:16. Both verses list the Arvadites among the descendants of Canaan, the son of Ham, in the "Table of Nations," the record of how the families of the earth spread out after…

h7218.g: beginning, beginnings, chief, chiefs, companies, company, first, head, heads, leader, leaders, own, sum, top, tops
h7218.sum: The Hebrew word rôʼsh means "head." Most often it is the physical head of a person or animal, but Hebrew speakers naturally extended the word to whatever stands first or highest. It can be the top of a mountain or tower, the beginning of a year or a river, the chief of a family or army, the finest of the spices, or the full sum of a count. Wherever it appears, it marks the place of first rank.

h7227.g: chief, Enough, enough, Great, great, Many, many, much, numerous
h7227.sum: The Hebrew word rav measures how much of something there is. It describes the many people, the great size, the long time, the large amount, and in some passages the older brother or the chief officer. The word itself is morally neutral. It can describe a crowd of enemies, a flood of water, a heap of treasure, or a pile of sin. Scripture's most important uses come when this same measuring word is turned toward God.…

h7233.sum: The Hebrew word rᵉbâbâh means "ten thousand" or "a myriad," the largest round number in ordinary Hebrew speech. It is often used to describe a crowd too large to count. The NKJV usually translates it as "ten thousand" or "ten thousands." Scripture often places it right after "thousand," so the number jumps upward line by line. That jump is the point. Five of Israel chase a hundred, but a hundred chase ten thousand.…

h7257.g: lay, lie, lies, Lying, lying, make
h7257.sum: The Hebrew verb râbats describes an animal folding its legs beneath it and settling to the ground. Sheep lie down in a pasture, a donkey sinks under a heavy load, a mother bird sits on her eggs, and a lion stretches out in its den. The posture is the same each time. Context decides whether it means safety, exhaustion, protection, menace, or royal ease. When the verb takes a causative form, it means "to make lie…

h7272.sum: The Hebrew word regel is the ordinary Old Testament word for "foot" or "leg." It names the feet that travelers washed, the feet that stood on holy ground, and the legs of furniture in the tabernacle. Because feet carry a person wherever they go, Scripture also uses the word for a person's walk and direction, for following someone, and even for counting "times." Feet run to evil or keep to God's path, slip in danger…

h7289.sum: The Hebrew word râdîyd names a woman's wide outer wrap: a large veil, shawl, or light cloak that covered her head and shoulders. It appears only twice in the Old Testament. The NKJV translates it "veil" in Song of Solomon 5:7 and "robes" in Isaiah 3:23. A garment like this gave the woman who wore it covering and protection in public.

h7291.g: chased, persecute, persecuted, persecutors, Pursue, pursue, pursued, pursuer, pursuers, pursues, pursuing, You
h7291.sum: Râdaph is the Hebrew verb for running after something in order to catch it. It describes armies chasing a beaten enemy, a hunter tracking game, a hostile man hounding the innocent, and a person who gives himself wholeheartedly to a goal. Most often the word sounds dangerous. Pharaoh's chariots pursue Israel to the sea, Saul hunts David through the wilderness, and the psalmists cry out against those who persecute…

h7292.sum: The Hebrew verb râhab describes pressing forward with strong, surging force. It means acting boldly, pressing hard, overwhelming someone, or pushing past boundaries that should be honored. This word appears only four times in the Old Testament. In each place the NKJV chooses a different English word: "bold," "Plead," "overcome," and "insolent." All four share the same energy of force pressing against resistance.…

h730.sum: The Hebrew word ʼerez means "cedar." In Scripture it almost always refers to the great cedars of Lebanon, which grew tall, rooted deep, stayed green through the year, and produced fragrant wood that resisted rot. Kings prized cedar as one of the finest timbers. David lived in "a house of cedar," Solomon lined the Temple with it until "there was no stone to be seen," and the priests of Israel used a piece of cedar…

h7307.g: breath, own, side, sides, Spirit, spirit, spirits, wind, winds
h7307.sum: Rûwach is the Hebrew word for moving air. Depending on the setting, the Old Testament uses it for the wind that sweeps across land and sea, the breath that keeps a creature alive, the inner spirit of a person, and the Spirit of God Himself. English needs several words to cover what Hebrew holds in one. Each use describes something unseen that is known by what it does: the sea parts, a body lives, a heart turns proud…

h7310.sum: The Hebrew noun rᵉvâyâh describes abundance as a state of being filled to the point of overflow. It belongs to a word family that speaks of drinking deeply and having one's thirst fully quenched. The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the Psalms, and both times God is the One who brings it about. In Psalm 23:5 David says, "My cup runs over," while the Lord spreads a table for him in front of his…

h7323.g: brought, couriers, guard, quickly, ran, Run, run, runner, runners, running, runs
h7323.sum: The Hebrew verb rûwts means to run . Scripture uses it for ordinary haste, like a servant hurrying to a well or a messenger racing from a battlefield. It also uses it as a title for the "runners" who guarded Israel's kings and the "couriers" who carried a king's decrees. Running in the Old Testament is rarely casual. People run when something matters: Abraham runs to greet his guests, Aaron runs into a plague with…

h7339.sum: The Hebrew word rᵉchôb names the broad open place of an ancient town: the plaza or public square, usually near the city gate, where people met, traded, judged cases, mourned, and celebrated. English Bibles render it "square," "open square," or "street." Its meaning comes from a word for being wide. It is the roomy, shared center of town, as opposed to a narrow lane between houses.

h7344.sum: Rehoboth is the name of three different places in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. The name means "broad places," "open spaces," or "streets," and comes from a Hebrew root meaning to be wide or roomy. The first Rehoboth is Rehoboth Ir, a city in Assyria listed among the early building projects connected with Nimrod (Genesis 10:11). The second is a well in the southern wilderness that Isaac named after two bitter disputes…

h7351.sum: The Hebrew word rᵉchîyṭ means rafter , one of the crossing timbers that hold up a roof or form a paneled ceiling. It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 1:17. There the bride says, "The beams of our houses are cedar, And our rafters of fir." Just before, she has said, "Also our bed is green" (Song of Solomon 1:16). Many readers take this to mean that the lovers are resting outdoors among living trees,…

h7353.sum: The Hebrew word râchêl means ewe , a grown female sheep. It is a specific word. Hebrew uses other words for a sheep or goat in general or for a ram, but râchêl names the mother of the flock, the animal whose wool, milk, and lambs kept a shepherd's household alive. Scripture uses it only four times. In Genesis the ewes are Jacob's working wealth, the breeding stock he guarded through twenty hard years. The Song of…

h7364.g: bathe, bathed, bathing, Wash, wash, Washed, washed, washes, washing
h7364.sum: The Hebrew verb râchats means to wash or bathe. It is used for water applied to a person's body, such as feet, hands, face or the whole body, and for the parts of an animal prepared for sacrifice. It first appears in Abraham's tent, where weary travelers were welcomed with water for their feet. It then becomes one of the working words of the tabernacle. Priests washed before they served, and unclean Israelites…

h7367.sum: The Hebrew word rachtsâh means washing . In the Bible it describes one familiar country scene: a flock of sheep climbing out of the water after being washed, their wool clean and white. The word appears only twice, and both times it comes from the bridegroom in the Song of Solomon as he praises his bride: "Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep Which have come up from the washing" (Song of Solomon 4:2). In Song…

h738.sum: The Hebrew word ʼărîy is the Old Testament's ordinary word for the lion, one of the strongest and most feared animals ancient Israel knew. Scripture uses it for real lions that raided flocks and killed travelers. It also uses it for the lions carved into Solomon's temple furnishings and set beside his throne. Most often, the lion serves as a picture. Judah is "a lion's whelp." The wicked lie in wait like lions. The…

h7381.sum: The Hebrew word rêyach simply means a smell: the scent of a field, of perfume, of a person's clothing, of water. Most often in Scripture, though, it rises from an altar. Again and again the Law describes an offering as "a sweet aroma to the LORD." That picture begins with Noah after the flood. God "smelled a soothing aroma" and resolved never again to destroy every living thing. It runs through the burnt offerings,…

h7384.sum: Riphath was the second-listed son of Gomer, a grandson of Japheth, and a great-grandson of Noah. His name appears only in the family lists of the nations that spread across the earth after the flood (Genesis 10:3; 1 Chronicles 1:6). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Riphath is an ancient tribal name, and no explanation of it has been established. Scripture records no deeds, speeches, or later history for him. He…

h7416.sum: The Hebrew word rimmôwn names the pomegranate, a red, crowned fruit packed with juicy seeds, and the small tree that bears it. Israel knew it as everyday food from the land God promised them. Scripture places it in a surprising range of settings. Pomegranates are carried back by the spies as proof that the land was good. They are woven onto the hem of the high priest's robe and cast in bronze by the hundreds on the…

h7447.sum: The Hebrew spelling râçîyç stands for two different words that Strong's lists under one number, H7447. Each appears in just one verse, and the two scenes could hardly feel more different. In Song of Solomon 5:2 the first describes the "drops of the night" on the hair of a lover who stands at his beloved's door, knocking and calling. In Amos 6:11 the second describes the "bits" a great house is broken into when the…

h7451.g: adversity, bad, calamity, deeds, Evil, evil, evils, harm, sad, trouble, troubles, wicked, wickedness, wild
h7451.sum: The Hebrew word raʻ is the Old Testament's ordinary word for what is bad. It is the opposite of "good," and it covers a wide range. It can describe moral wickedness: the evil a person plans, speaks, or does against God and neighbor. It can also describe what is harmful or painful without any sin implied, such as sickly cattle, a heavy task, a sad face, a dangerous animal, or a national disaster. English translations…

h7453.g: companion, companions, friend, friends, neighbor, neighbors, neighbor’s
h7453.sum: The Hebrew word rêaʻ names the person beside you. That may be the neighbor across the field boundary, the companion in the camp, the trusted friend whose counsel you seek, or even a lover. In its plainest use it simply means another . The Hebrew phrase a man to his rêaʻ is the ordinary way of saying one to another . The setting decides how close the relationship is, but the word always places one person in relation…

h7454.sum: The Hebrew word rêaʻ means a thought: what a person has in mind, including intentions and purposes. It is one of the rarest words in the Old Testament. It appears only twice, and both times in Psalm 139. In verse 2 David uses it for his own mind: "You understand my thought afar off." Fifteen verses later he uses it for God's mind: "How precious also are Your thoughts to me, O God!"

h7462.g: Feed, feed, feeding, feeds, keeper, pastured, Shepherd, shepherd, shepherded, shepherdess, shepherds, shepherd’s
h7462.sum: The Hebrew verb raah means to pasture a flock: to lead animals out to graze and look after them. When animals are the subject, it means to graze or feed. Used as a noun, it names the person who tends the flock, the shepherd or herdsman. The NKJV often translates the word as "feed," so a reader may not notice that "feed" and "shepherd" in the same verse can come from the same Hebrew word. Abram's herdsmen, Rachel,…

h7466.sum: Reu was the son of Peleg and the father of Serug, a descendant of Shem who lived in the generations after the Flood, in the era commonly associated with the scattering at Babel. His name probably means "friend" or "companion." It is generally connected with the Hebrew word for a friend or neighbor, though the derivation is not certain. Scripture records almost nothing about his life. Genesis 11:18–21 gives his…

h7467.sum: Reuel is a Hebrew personal name generally understood to mean "friend of God," formed from a word for "friend" or "companion" joined to El , "God." Four different men carry it in Scripture, and they should not be confused with one another. The first is a son of Esau by Basemath, Ishmael's daughter, who became the father of several clan chiefs in Edom (Genesis 36). The second is the priest of Midian who took in Moses…

h7474.sum: The Hebrew word raʻyâh is a tender term of endearment meaning darling , dear companion or beloved friend . It appears only nine times in the Bible, all in the Song of Solomon, and the NKJV translates it "my love" each time. It is the bridegroom's affectionate name for his bride in the Song's dialogue. He normally speaks it to her directly, sometimes in words she remembers; in Song of Solomon 2:2 he uses it to…

h7484.sum: Raamah was a son of Cush and a grandson of Ham, named in the Table of Nations after the Flood (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9). His name later stands for the people and region descended from him, an Arabian trading nation that Ezekiel lists among the merchants who enriched the city of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:22). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Some connect it to a Hebrew root associated with thunder or trembling,…

h7488.sum: The Hebrew word raʻănân describes a tree that is leafy, luxuriant and full of life. English Bibles usually translate it green , but the word describes vitality more than color. It also describes "fresh oil" (Psalm 92:10) and the righteous who stay fresh and flourishing in old age. The opposite of raʻănân is a branch that withers or a land struck by drought.

h7502.sum: The Hebrew verb râphad means to spread something out, especially to lay out a place to lie on, as when someone makes a bed or spreads a couch. It can also carry the related idea of propping someone up or supporting them on what has been spread beneath them. The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in poetry. Those few uses carry a surprising range of feeling.

h7503.w: Slacken, Let Go, Leave, Be Still
h7503.sum: The Hebrew verb râphâh pictures a grip loosening and hands dropping. It can describe hands going limp with fear, workers growing slack, a person releasing what they held, or someone stopping what they were doing. English translations render it in many ways, including "feeble," "idle," "let go," "leave," "cease," "restrain," and "be still." Underneath every one of these renderings is the same picture of hands that…

h7507.sum: The Hebrew word rᵉphîydâh names a supporting part of a royal carriage. Translators have understood it as the base, the back, or a railing, and the exact part cannot be fixed with certainty. The word appears only once in the entire Bible, in the Song of Solomon's description of King Solomon's wedding procession. The NKJV translates it "support": "He made its pillars of silver, Its support of gold, Its seat of purple"…

h7514.sum: The Hebrew word râphaq means to lean on someone or to support oneself against someone. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 8:5, where the bride comes "up from the wilderness, Leaning upon her beloved." Because Scripture uses the word only once, its meaning comes from this single scene, and the scene is a rich one. A woman comes up out of the wilderness. She is not walking alone or carried…

h7528.sum: The Hebrew verb râtsaph means to fit together, to pave, or to inlay. It describes the careful work of setting pieces side by side until they form one finished surface, the way a craftsman lays a patterned floor or a mosaic. The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 3:10. There it describes the inside of King Solomon's carriage, in a poem that celebrates his wedding day: "Its interior paved…

h753.sum: The Hebrew noun ʼôrek means "length." Most often it gives the long measurement of something God told His people to build: Noah's ark, the tabernacle and its furniture, Solomon's temple, and the temple Ezekiel saw in vision. Again and again Scripture records "the length shall be..." because God was not vague about the places where He would save, meet, and dwell with His people. Holiness came with exact dimensions.

h7541.sum: The Hebrew word raqqâh names the temple, the soft, flat place on the side of the head between the eye and the ear. It appears only five times in the Old Testament, in two very different scenes. In Judges it marks the exact spot where Jael drove a tent peg into Sisera, the commander of the army of Jabin, the Canaanite king who had harshly oppressed Israel for twenty years. In the Song of Solomon it describes the…

h7544.sum: The Hebrew noun reqach means spice . It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 8:2, where the bride says to the one she loves, "I would cause you to drink of spiced wine, Of the juice of my pomegranate." The NKJV renders it with the single word "spiced." Spiced wine was not everyday wine. It was ordinary wine blended with costly aromatic ingredients, a drink fit for a special guest, and the bride names…

h7565.sum: The Hebrew word resheph is a rare poetic noun for a flash of fire, and for things that strike suddenly the way a flash does. It appears seven times, in six verses. Its uses fall into three main kinds: a flame or spark (Job 5:7; Song of Solomon 8:6), a burning sickness such as plague or fever (Deuteronomy 32:24; Habakkuk 3:5), and a flashing bolt such as lightning or arrows (Psalm 78:48; Psalm 76:3). In their…

h758.sum: Aram is the Hebrew name for the Arameans and their homeland, the cluster of kingdoms north and northeast of Israel centered on Damascus. The NKJV usually translates it "Syria." The same name also belongs to three individuals: a son of Shem in the table of nations, a grandson of Abraham's brother Nahor, and a little-known man of the tribe of Asher. The name is traditionally understood to mean "high" or "exalted,"…

h7585.sum: Sheol is the Old Testament's name for the realm of the dead, and often for the power of death itself. Righteous and wicked alike speak of going down to it. Jacob expected to go there grieving for Joseph, psalmists cry out when its cords tighten around them, and prophets announce that proud kings and nations will be brought down to it in judgment. English Bibles render the word "grave," "hell," "pit," or simply…

h7586.sum: Saul was the first king of Israel, a son of Kish from the tribe of Benjamin, whose reign marks the troubled passage from the days of the judges to the house of David. His name means "asked for." The Hebrew is drawn from the ordinary verb "to ask," and the meaning is woven into the story itself. Israel asked for a king like all the nations (1 Samuel 8), and God gave them a man whose very name said "asked for." Paul…

h7614.sum: Sheba is the name most closely associated with a wealthy trading people of southern Arabia, the Sabeans, though not every biblical Sheba group can simply be identified with that southern kingdom. Scripture traces the name through three separate genealogical lines: a descendant of Ham through Cush, a descendant of Shem through Joktan, and a grandson of Abraham through Keturah. The meaning of the name itself is…

h7626.g: rod, Scepter, scepter, scepters, spears, staff, tribe, tribes
h7626.sum: The Hebrew word shêbeṭ names a stick or rod of wood. What it means in a given passage depends on whose hand holds it. A king holds it as a scepter , a shepherd as a rod to guard and count his flock, and a father or master as a rod of correction. A warrior can carry it as a club or a dart. Most often in the Old Testament it names a tribe of Israel, a household gathered under the authority its leader's staff…

h765.sum: Aran was a Horite, one of the early inhabitants of Mount Seir, the rugged highland south of the Dead Sea that later became the land of Edom. Scripture names him only twice, both times in the same short line of genealogy: "The sons of Dishan were Uz and Aran" (1 Chronicles 1:42; compare Genesis 36:28). His father Dishan was one of the sons of Seir the Horite, which makes Aran a grandson of Seir. The meaning of his…

h7650.g: cause, made, make, oath, oaths, Swear, swear, swears, swore, sworn
h7650.sum: The Hebrew verb shâbaʻ means to swear, or to bind oneself with an oath. It can also mean to put someone else under oath, which the NKJV often translates "charge." In Scripture, swearing has nothing to do with foul language. It is a solemn affirmation or commitment, the most serious guarantee a person can give that his word is true or that he will do what he has promised. The words can be very brief: when Abimelech…

h7688.sum: The Hebrew verb shâgach means to gaze, to look intently, or to peer. It describes an attentive look at something. How long the look lasts and what it leads to come from each passage, not from the verb alone. The verb appears only three times in the Old Testament, and each time a different person is looking. In Psalm 33:14 the LORD looks from His heavenly dwelling "On all the inhabitants of the earth." In Song of…

h7699.sum: The Hebrew word shad means breast , most often a woman's breast as the place where a child is nursed. Scripture uses the word in a small number of passages, but it reaches across a wide range of human experience. It appears in a newborn's first trust, a young woman's coming of age, the delight of married love, the cruelty of famine and siege, and the warmth of a mother's comfort. The Song of Solomon accounts for a…

h7725.g: Again, again, back, been, Bring, bring, bringing, brings, brought, cause, certainly, come, Go, go, had, has, make, may, must, recall, repaid, Repay, repay, repent, Rescue, respond, Restore, restore, restored, restores, Return, return, returned, returning, returns, revoke, Turn, turn, turned, turning, turns, went, You, you
h7725.sum: The Hebrew verb shûwb means to turn back or return. In daily life it describes a traveler heading home, a dove flying back to the ark, or a lender handing back a borrowed cloak. It can also mean to bring something back: to restore stolen property, recover captives, or give back an answer. From these ordinary uses the Old Testament draws one of its central pictures of life with God. Sin is a turning away from Him,…

h7732.sum: Shobal is the name of at least two different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused. The first is a Horite chief, a son of Seir, whose people lived in the hill country of Seir before Esau's descendants took it over (Genesis 36:20–29; 1 Chronicles 1:38–40). The second is a man of the tribe of Judah, a son of Hur and a descendant of Hezron's son Caleb. Chronicles calls him "Shobal the father of…

h7744.sum: Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah, Abraham's wife, also called a concubine. Genesis introduces her after Sarah's death; the traditional reading places the marriage then, though the text does not settle its timing. He is named last among her six sons in Genesis 25:2 and again in 1 Chronicles 1:32. His name is probably related to a Hebrew verb meaning "to sink down" or "to bow down," which suggests a sense such as…

h775.sum: Arphaxad (also spelled Arpachshad) was a son of Shem and a grandson of Noah. He was born "two years after the flood" (Genesis 11:10), so he belongs to the first generation of the world that came out of the ark. The meaning of his name is uncertain. It may not be Hebrew in origin. Its last letters resemble Kesed , the root behind the Hebrew name for the Chaldeans, so some scholars have suggested a link to Chaldea or…

h7759.sum: "Shulamite" is the name given to the bride in the Song of Solomon. It appears only twice in the Bible, and both times in the same verse, Song of Solomon 6:13, at a high point of the poem: "Return, return, O Shulamite; Return, return, that we may look upon you!" It reads more like a title than a personal name, and its origin is debated. It may point to a home region, much like "Shunammite." It may also be a feminine…

h776.g: countries, country, Earth, earth, ground, Land, land, lands, O, own
h776.sum: ʼErets is the ordinary Hebrew word for the earth beneath our feet. It can mean the whole created world, a particular country such as Egypt or Canaan, or simply the ground where someone bows or falls. It is one of the most common nouns in the Old Testament. It opens the Bible, where God created the heavens and the earth, and it carries the story through Abraham's call, Israel's inheritance, exile, and the promise of…

h7760.g: appoint, appointed, charges, Consider, consider, determined, established, formed, gave, give, had, has, made, Make, make, makes, performed, placed, Put, put, puts, Set, set, sets, up, when, you
h7760.sum: The Hebrew verb sûwm means to put, set, or place something where it belongs. It can also mean to make, appoint, or establish. It is one of the Old Testament's everyday working verbs. People use it when they put food on a table, set a stone upright, put on sackcloth, or appoint a king. Because the word is so ordinary, its weightier uses can be easy to miss. When God is the one doing the putting, the word describes…

h7776.sum: The Hebrew word shûwʻâl names the fox. It also covers the jackal, the fox's larger cousin that runs in packs and feeds on carrion. The word appears only seven times, in six verses of the Old Testament (Song of Solomon 2:15 uses it twice), and in nearly every case the animal turns up where something valuable is left unguarded or has already been lost. Foxes slip into a vineyard to spoil the young grapes. They prowl…

h7784.sum: The Hebrew word shûwq means street , the public lanes of a town where people walk, trade, meet, and pass one another. It appears only four times in the Old Testament, all in the poetry of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Solomon. In each passage the street is shared public space, outside the private shelter of the home, and each passage gives it its own image.

h7785.sum: The Hebrew word shôwq means leg . It can mean the upper leg, or thigh, of an animal, or the legs of a person. In the laws of worship it names the right thigh of the peace offering, the portion God claimed for Himself and gave to His priests "by a statute forever" (Leviticus 7:34). The same word appears when Samuel had a specially reserved thigh served to Saul at a feast, the day before he anointed him (1 Samuel…

h7789.sum: The Hebrew verb shûwr means to see. More exactly, it means to gaze, watch closely, or keep someone or something in view. It is a rare and mostly poetic word. Most of its uses come from the book of Job, with the rest in Balaam's oracles, the Song of Solomon, Jeremiah, and Hosea. The NKJV renders it in several ways: "behold," "see," "perceive," "regard," "observed," and even "lurk." That range shows how much depends…

h7805.sum: The Hebrew verb shâzaph means to catch sight of, look on, or gaze at something. It is one of the Bible's rarest words for seeing. It appears only three times, all in poetry, and each time a different created eye is looking. In Job 20:9 a human eye sees a proud man prospering and then cannot find him. In Job 28:7 the falcon, a bird famous for its keen sight, has never seen the hidden path the miner cuts to buried…

h7837.sum: The Hebrew word shachar means the dawn: the first light breaking over the horizon as night gives way to day. Most English Bibles translate it as "morning," "day," "dawn," or "daybreak." In the narrative books, the word often marks the moment when a long night ends and God's purpose moves forward. The angels hurry Lot out of Sodom at dawn. Jacob wrestles until the day breaks and leaves with a new name. Israel rises…

h7840.sum: The Hebrew word shᵉcharchôreth means dark or dark in complexion . It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 1:6. There a young woman stands before the "daughters of Jerusalem" and pleads, "Do not look upon me, because I am dark, Because the sun has tanned me." She explains her dark skin by the sun and by the outdoor work her angry brothers forced on her in the vineyards. Meanwhile, as she puts it, "my…

h7857.g: off, overflow, overflowed, overflowing, rinsed, rushes, someone, swept, wash
h7857.sum: The Hebrew verb shâṭaph describes water in motion that carries things away. In ordinary life it meant rinsing: a bronze pot or a wooden bowl was rinsed in water, and a bloody chariot was washed at a pool. Its larger meaning is the rushing flood that overflows its banks and sweeps everything before it. The prophets used that flood to picture invading armies and the judgment of God. The psalmists used it for trouble…

h7892.sum: The Hebrew word shîyr means "song." It can name a particular song, the act of singing, or the organized music of Israel's worship. The word itself is ordinary. Laban uses it for the farewell party he says Jacob denied him, and Isaiah uses it for a harlot's tune. Yet the Bible's most important uses gather around what God has done. Israel's first song to the LORD rises on the far shore of the Red Sea. Moses writes a…

h790.sum: Eshban was a Horite, one of the sons of Dishon. His family belonged to the people who lived in the mountains of Seir, south of the Dead Sea, before the descendants of Esau took the land. He appears only twice in Scripture, in Genesis 36:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:41, both times as a name in a family list. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Older proposals link it to Hebrew words for "fire" or "understanding," but…

h7909.sum: The Hebrew word shakkûwl describes someone who has lost their young. It is not the ordinary word for a woman who could never conceive. It describes a mother whose offspring have been taken from her. The NKJV renders it "robbed," "deprived," "bereaved," and "barren." In four places it pictures the loss of young: three times a mother bear robbed of her cubs, and once wives left bereaved of their children in Jeremiah's…

h7925.sum: The Hebrew verb shâkam means to rise early or to make an early start. In the NKJV it nearly always appears as "early," usually in the familiar phrase "rose early in the morning." The word tells us when and how promptly something began. In the Bible's narratives it marks people who did not wait. Abraham set out at dawn with Isaac and the wood for the offering, and Joshua rose early to lead Israel to the Jordan and…

h7937.g: become, drunk, Made, made, Make, make
h7937.sum: The Hebrew word shâkar means to be drunk or to drink until one is full. Sometimes it describes literal drunkenness, as when Noah drank wine from his vineyard and lay uncovered in his tent. Sometimes it describes glad, generous feasting, as when Joseph's brothers "drank and were merry with him." Most often, especially in the prophets, it becomes a picture of a person or nation overwhelmed, staggering and helpless…

h7965.g: health, Peace, peace, safety, welfare, well
h7965.sum: The Hebrew word shâlôwm, usually translated "peace," describes well-being, safety and wholeness. Depending on the passage it can mean safety on a journey, health in the body, prosperity in a household, friendly relations between neighbors, an end to war, and the settled trust of a heart resting in God. When an Israelite asked, "Is he well?" (Genesis 29:6), he was asking about a person's shâlôwm. Not every use means…

h7971.g: away, cast, depart, down, forth, gave, go, had, Let, let, lets, out, Send, send, sending, sends, Sent, sent, set, Stretch, stretch, stretched, stretches
h7971.sum: The Hebrew word shâlach is the Old Testament's ordinary verb for sending. It describes something moving out from a person toward a purpose. A king sends a messenger, a man stretches out his hand, a master lets a slave go free, and a husband sends a wife out of his house. The word itself does not say whether the sending brings blessing, grief, or judgment. The story around it decides that.

h7973.sum: The Hebrew word shelach has two distinct senses. Most often it names a hand weapon or missile: the weapon in the hand of a guard, the arms Hezekiah stockpiled, and the weapon Nehemiah's builders held while they laid stones. In Job the same word becomes a picture of sudden death, the strike that ends a life cut off from God. Then, once, in the Song of Solomon, it describes something entirely different: the growing…

h7974.sum: Shelah was a son of Arphaxad and grandson of Shem. He lived in the generations after the Flood and was the father of Eber. His name, Hebrew Shelach (שֶׁלַח), comes from a root meaning "to send." Its exact meaning as a personal name is uncertain. The noun can mean "a missile" or "weapon," something sent out, and it can also mean "a shoot" or "sprout," something a plant sends forth. Genesis records nothing he did…

h7979.sum: The Hebrew word shulchân means “table,” the ordinary piece of furniture on which food was set out. Scripture uses it for family and royal tables, for the gold-covered table in the tabernacle, for work tables in Ezekiel's temple, and even for the altar itself. In its most important uses, the table pictures fellowship and intimacy with God: being welcomed into His presence, sharing life with Him, living on His…

h7982.sum: The Hebrew word sheleṭ names a shield. It is a rare word, appearing only seven times in the Old Testament, and its exact shape, size and material are not certain. What stands out is where these shields appear: gold shields taken in battle, shields kept in the temple, and shields hung on towers and city walls where everyone could see the strength of the people who owned them. Almost every use links strength with…

h8008.sum: The Hebrew word salmâh names an ordinary garment, especially the outer cloak an Israelite wore by day and slept under at night. For a poor man, this cloak might be the only blanket he owned. Scripture uses this everyday item to show how closely God pays attention to ordinary life. God commands that a poor neighbor's cloak, taken as a pledge for a loan, be returned before sunset. He promises to hear the cry of the…

h8010.sum: Solomon was the son of King David and Bathsheba and the third king to rule over all twelve tribes of Israel. He reigned forty years from Jerusalem, roughly 970 to 931 BC. His name appears to come from the Hebrew word family of shalom , peace , though its exact form and shade of meaning are uncertain. What Scripture makes plain is the association of his name with peace. Before Solomon was born, God told David, "His…

h802.g: Each, each, O, own, wife, wife’s, wives, Woman, woman, woman’s, women, women’s
h802.sum: Ishshâh is the ordinary Hebrew word for a woman. Hebrew has no separate word for "wife," so the same word names both a woman and a married woman. "His woman" means "his wife," and context decides which English word fits. The word runs from the creation of Eve to Malachi's teaching about marriage. It names the matriarchs and the women protected in Israel's laws. It names mothers, widows, prophetesses, queens, and the…

h8026.sum: Sheleph is one of the thirteen sons of Joktan named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:26) and again in the Chronicler's opening genealogy (1 Chronicles 1:20). He belongs to the family of Shem through Eber, and his descendants were among the Joktanite peoples whose homeland Genesis describes as stretching "from Mesha as you go toward Sephar, the mountain of the east" (Genesis 10:30). His name is commonly connected…

h8034.sum: The Hebrew word shêm means "name." It is the ordinary word for what a person, place, or thing is called, from the rivers of Eden to the sons of Jacob. In Hebrew usage, though, a name goes further than a label. It stands for how someone is known: their reputation and their remembered identity. Men of great reputation are "men of renown," a ruined reputation is a "bad name," and a man's name surviving in Israel means…

h8035.sum: Shem was the son of Noah, the brother of Ham and Japheth, and one of the eight people who came through the Flood alive. His name is spelled exactly like the ordinary Hebrew word for "name," and it carries the sense of renown or reputation. That simple meaning becomes surprisingly important in Genesis. The builders of Babel tried to "make a name" for themselves and were scattered. The very next section of Genesis…

h804.sum: Asshur is the Hebrew name for Assyria. Scripture uses the name for a man, a land, and an empire: Asshur the son of Shem (Genesis 10:22), the land along the upper Tigris that bore his name, and the empire that rose from that land to dominate the ancient Near East. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Older lexical tradition proposes "a step" or "successful," but neither meaning is firmly established. What is clear…

h8040.sum: The Hebrew word sᵉmôʼwl means the left : the left hand, the left side, or a leftward direction. Because Israelites oriented themselves facing east, toward the sunrise, the left could also mean north . The word is plain and physical. It names which hand Jacob laid on a grandson's head, which side of the temple a pillar stood on, and which way a traveler must not turn. Scripture often pairs it with the right to…

h8048.sum: Shammah is a name shared by several different men in the Old Testament, and the first task is keeping them apart. One is an Edomite chief, a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:13, 17; 1 Chronicles 1:37). Another is the third son of Jesse of Bethlehem, an older brother of David, who passed before Samuel and heard the prophet say, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one" (1 Samuel 16:9). A third, Shammah the son of Agee the…

h8055.g: glad, him, made, Make, make, makes, pleased, Rejoice, rejoice, rejoiced, rejoices, rejoicing
h8055.sum: The Hebrew verb sâmach means to rejoice or be glad, and in some uses to make someone else glad. It can describe quiet gladness of heart, as when Aaron would be "glad in his heart" to see Moses (Exodus 4:14), but it very often describes joy that shows. People eat, sing, shout and celebrate with it. The Old Testament uses the word for families at the table, crowds at a coronation and worshipers at a festival. It also…

h8057.g: Gladness, gladness, Joy, joy, pleasure, rejoiced
h8057.sum: The Hebrew noun simchâh is one of the Old Testament's main words for joy. NKJV usually translates it "joy" or "gladness," and sometimes "mirth," "pleasure," or "rejoicing." It can describe the gladness a person feels in the heart, and it can also describe the joy people express together through singing, feasting, music, and shouting. Scripture uses the word for ordinary human happiness at harvests and weddings, and…

h8072.sum: Samlah was an early king of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. He is the fifth ruler named in the Edomite king list of Genesis 36, and the same list is repeated in 1 Chronicles 1. His name most likely means "garment" or "mantle." It matches the ordinary Hebrew word for a cloak or wrapper, though Scripture never comments on why he bore it. The Bible tells us only three things about him: he came from a place called…

h8081.sum: Shemen is the Hebrew word for oil, above all the olive oil pressed from the fruit of Israel's hillsides. In Scripture, the anointing oil becomes one of the clearest pictures of the Holy Spirit consecrating and empowering people for God's service. Moses poured it on Aaron's head to set him apart as priest. Samuel poured it on Saul and told him that the Spirit of the LORD would come upon him. When Samuel anointed…

h8084.sum: The Hebrew word shᵉmônîym simply means eighty . Scripture uses it to count years, people, soldiers, workers, and days. Sometimes it stands alone, as when Moses is eighty years old, and sometimes it forms part of a larger number, such as the 185,000 Assyrians struck down in one night or the "four hundred and eightieth year" after the Exodus. The number carries no hidden meaning of its own. Its importance comes from…

h8085.g: cause, certainly, has, have, Hear, hear, heard, hearing, hears, heeds, Listen, listen, listened, listening, listens, made, Make, make, may, Obey, obey, obeyed, obeying, obeys, Proclaim, proclaim, proclaimed, proclaims, sound, understand, you
h8085.sum: Shâmaʻ is the Hebrew verb behind "hear," "listen," "heed," and "obey" in the Old Testament. It begins with sound reaching the ear, but it rarely stays there. In Scripture, hearing God means taking His word in, understanding it, and acting on it. Very often, when the NKJV says "obey," this is the word behind it, so the vocabulary itself ties hearing to obeying. When Samuel tells Saul that "to obey is better than…

h809.sum: The Hebrew word ʼăshîyshâh names a cake of pressed raisins: a sweet, compact food made from dried grapes. It was a treat for special occasions, valued for its sweetness and the quick strength it gave. The word occurs 5 times in 5 verses of the Hebrew Bible. Four of them are clearly rendered as food in the NKJV, and each carries weight. When David brought the ark of God into Jerusalem, he gave every Israelite, man…

h81.sum: The Hebrew word ʼăbâqâh means fine aromatic powder: costly spices ground to dust and used to perfume people, clothing and surroundings. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 3:6, where a royal wedding procession rises out of the wilderness "Perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, With all the merchant's fragrant powders." Because the word occurs only once, everything we learn about it comes from that…

h8104.g: because, care, careful, Guard, guard, guarded, guards, has, have, heed, Keep, keep, keeper, keepers, keeping, Keeps, keeps, kept, Observe, observe, Preserve, preserve, preserved, preserves, regard, Take, take, took, watch, watched, watches, watching, watchman, watchmen
h8104.sum: The Hebrew verb shâmar means to keep something with careful attention. It describes the alert care of a guard over a person, a flock, a gate, or a holy place, and the careful obedience of someone who treasures God's words and does them. English Bibles render it "keep," "guard," "preserve," "watch," "observe," "take heed," and "beware." The verb's "-ing" form also names people by their work: keeper, watchman,…

h811.sum: The Hebrew word ʼeshkôwl means cluster : a bunch of grapes, dates, or blossoms growing together on one stem. It is an ordinary farm word. Scripture uses it in a few vivid places, and each time it shows what kind of fruit is present and what that fruit reveals.

h8121.sum: The Hebrew word shemesh means "sun." It names the great light God set in the sky to rule the day. Because the sun dominated every ancient sky, Scripture also uses it to mark direction and time. Its rising meant east, its going down meant west, and sunset closed the working day. The biblical writers return to the sun again and again to say who God is. He made it, He commands it, and He alone deserves the worship that…

h8127.sum: The Hebrew word shên means "tooth." Scripture uses it for the teeth of people and animals. It also uses it for ivory, since an elephant's tusk is a tooth, and for things shaped like teeth, such as the prongs of a fork or a jagged point of rock. Because teeth are what bite, chew, and tear, the word shows up wherever the Bible talks about appetite and power. The law protects a servant's tooth. The psalmists ask God to…

h813.sum: Ashkenaz appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, but those few verses carry the name from the first generations after the flood to the fall of Babylon. In Genesis 10:3 and 1 Chronicles 1:6, Ashkenaz is a son of Gomer, a grandson of Japheth, and a great-grandson of Noah. In Jeremiah 51:27 the name has become a kingdom, one of the northern powers God summons against Babylon alongside Ararat and Minni. The…

h8144.sum: The Hebrew word shânîy means "scarlet": the brilliant red dye, the thread or yarn colored with it, and cloth made from that yarn. In the ancient world, scarlet was costly and hard to produce, so it marked honor, wealth, and beauty. Most of its uses appear in Exodus, where God commands scarlet yarn to be woven with blue, purple, and fine linen into the curtains of His tabernacle and the garments of the high priest.…

h8147.sum: Shᵉnayim is the ordinary Hebrew word for "two." It counts people, animals, objects, and years, and it is often translated "both," "pair," or "couple." In combination with other words it also produces "twelve," "twelfth," "second," "twice," "double," and larger numbers such as "sixty-two." Most of its uses are plain counting. Two sons, two pillars, and two loaves need no hidden meaning.

h8149.sum: Senir is a name for the great mountain on Israel's far northern horizon, the snow-topped height better known as Mount Hermon, northeast of the Sea of Galilee. Moses explains that the Amorites called Hermon "Senir," while the Sidonians called it "Sirion" (Deuteronomy 3:9). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Some scholars suggest "coat of mail" or "snow mountain," both of which suit a high, armored-looking ridge…

h8165.sum: Seir is the rugged mountain country south of the Dead Sea that God gave to Esau and his descendants, the Edomites. The same Hebrew name also belongs to Seir the Horite, an ancestor of the people who lived there before Esau. It also names a separate Mount Seir on Judah's northern border. The name is commonly understood to mean "hairy" or "shaggy," probably describing rough, brush-covered hill country. Hebrew readers…

h8179.sum: The Hebrew word shaʻar means "gate," the opening in the wall of a city, a temple court, a palace, or even the boundary of a camp. In ancient Israel the city gate was where public life happened. Elders sat there to judge cases, business was settled there, and news arrived there first. Kings took their seats there. Because so much passed through the gate, the word could stand for the whole town. When Deuteronomy…

h8181.sum: Sêʻâr is the ordinary Hebrew word for hair, whether on a person's head and body or on an animal's hide woven into a garment. It describes everyday things: a baby's appearance at birth, a bride's beauty, a priest's examination of a skin disease. Because hair is so visible and so personal, Scripture also uses it to show what is happening between people and God. In Leviticus, the priest reads hair to tell whether a…

h8193.g: bank, border, edge, language, lip, lips, shore
h8193.sum: The Hebrew word sâphâh means "lip," and in Scripture it reaches outward from there. It names the lips of the body, the speech and language that come from the lips, and the edge of almost anything: the bank of a river, the shore of a sea, the brim of a basin, or the hem of a curtain or garment. English translations use many different words for it, so readers rarely notice that "language" at Babel, "lips" in Proverbs,…

h8195.sum: Shepho was a Horite of Mount Seir, the rugged highland south of the Dead Sea that later became Edom. He was the son of the chief Shobal and a grandson of Seir the Horite. Genesis does not list Shepho himself among the chiefs. Genesis spells his name Shepho (Genesis 36:23), and 1 Chronicles spells it Shephi (1 Chronicles 1:40). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Lexicons link it to a Hebrew root meaning "to sweep…

h8248.g: butler, cupbearer, cupbearers, drink, drinks, gave, give, make, Water, water, watered, waters
h8248.sum: The Hebrew verb shâqâh means to water or to give drink . It describes one party supplying water or another drink to someone or something else. A mist waters the ground in Eden, Rebekah draws water for a stranger's camels, and Moses waters the flock of the seven daughters of the priest of Midian. The same word supplies the title of Pharaoh's "butler," the official whose work was to give the king his drink. Scripture…

h8259.g: down, Look, look, looked, Looks, looks
h8259.sum: The Hebrew word shâqaph means to look down or look out from a high or sheltered place. Someone leans out of a window, a mountain peak looks over the valley below, or the Lord looks down from heaven. The word always assumes a vantage point. The one who looks is above the scene or set apart from it, and what they see is spread out beneath them.

h8286.sum: Serug was a descendant of Shem who lived in the generations between the flood and Abraham. He was the son of Reu, the father of Nahor, the grandfather of Terah, and the great-grandfather of Abram. His name most likely comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to intertwine," and some interpreters render it "branch" or "shoot." That meaning is a probable derivation rather than a settled one. Genesis records only a few facts…

h8289.sum: Sharon is a broad, level region in the land of Israel. In most passages it means the fertile coastal plain that runs along the Mediterranean from around Joppa north toward Mount Carmel. The name is generally understood to come from a Hebrew root meaning to be level or straight , so Sharon most likely means the plain or the level land . Scripture also mentions "the common-lands of Sharon" east of the Jordan in the…

h8326.sum: The Hebrew word shôrer means navel , the small mark at the center of the body where every person was once joined to a mother's life. It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:2. There a bridegroom praises his bride: "Your navel is a rounded goblet; it lacks no blended beverage. Your waist is a heap of wheat set about with lilies." Because it is used only once, this single verse carries the word's whole…

h833.sum: The Hebrew verb ʼâshar has two sides. Most often it means to call someone blessed: to look at a life and say aloud that it is happy, favored, and well. Leah uses it when her son Asher is born. Children use it of their mother in Proverbs 31, and God uses it when He promises that the nations will call His repentant people blessed. In other passages the same verb means to walk, to go forward, or to guide along a way.…

h8336.sum: The Hebrew word shêsh names fine white linen. It was a bleached, carefully woven fabric that took great labor to make and was worn in palaces and used in God's sanctuary. The same word is also used for a white stone, which the NKJV translates as "marble." Dictionaries usually treat this as an extended use, though the Bible itself does not explain how one word came to cover both. Most of its uses are in Exodus.…

h8346.sum: The Hebrew word shishshîym is the ordinary number "sixty." It has no hidden meaning of its own. It counts years, soldiers, cities, offerings, and cubits, and it appears inside larger numbers such as sixty-five or three hundred sixty. Its interest for Bible readers comes from where Scripture places it. A number in the Bible is part of a record kept by a God who pays attention to exact years, real people, and actual…

h8352.sum: Seth was the third named son of Adam and Eve, born after Cain murdered Abel. Genesis itself explains his name. Eve named him Seth because, she said, "God has appointed another seed for me instead of Abel, whom Cain killed" (Genesis 4:25). The name is tied to the Hebrew verb meaning "to put, set, or appoint," so Seth carries the sense of "appointed" or "set in place." His birth answered the first great crisis after…

h8354.g: certainly, drank, Drink, drink, drinkers, drinking, drinks, drunk
h8354.sum: The Hebrew verb shâthâh is the Old Testament's ordinary word for to drink . It describes the most basic act of staying alive. Travelers drink at wells, armies drink at streams, families drink at feasts, and thirsty people drink when God provides water in the desert. Because no one can live without drinking, Scripture uses this simple word to show how completely human beings depend on God. Israel in the wilderness…

h8380.sum: The Hebrew word tâʼôwm means twin . It describes two children born together from one pregnancy, a pair of young animals born together, and, by extension, two things joined so closely that they function as a matched pair. The NKJV translates it "twins" in Genesis and the Song of Solomon and "coupled" in the building instructions for the tabernacle. The word appears only eight times in six verses. Because it is so…

h8382.sum: The Hebrew verb tâʼam means to be double or to come in matching pairs. The Song of Solomon uses it twice (4:2; 6:6), where the NKJV translates it as "bears twins." The bridegroom praises his bride's smile by comparing her teeth to a flock of freshly washed sheep, "every one of which bears twins, and none is barren among them" (Song 4:2). The picture is of a smile where every tooth has its matching partner and none…

h8384.sum: The Hebrew word tᵉʼên means fig or fig tree . In ancient Israel the fig was a staple food and a familiar shade tree. A family could plant one only if it expected to stay on its land for years. Scripture often pairs the fig with the vine, and the two together came to picture a household at rest. To sit "under his vine and his fig tree" meant to live safely on your own land, with enough to eat and no enemy at the…

h8422.sum: Tubal is the fifth listed son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah. His name also became the name of a people who descended from him. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Some connect it with a root meaning "to bring" or "brought," but the Bible gives no explanation of the name, and no derivation is settled. Tubal appears only eight times in Scripture. Genesis and 1 Chronicles list him among the founders of the…

h8425.sum: Togarmah is named only four times in Scripture, but the name covers a long distance. He first appears in the Table of Nations as the third listed son of Gomer and a great-grandson of Noah through Japheth (Genesis 10:3; 1 Chronicles 1:6). In Ezekiel the name has become a people, "the house of Togarmah," a northern nation that traded horses, steeds, and mules with the merchant city of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:14). Ezekiel…

h8432.sum: The Hebrew word tâvek means midst , middle or among . It names the center of something, such as the middle of a river, the inside of a camp, or a place among a group of people. It is an ordinary word. Scripture uses it for a garden, a sea, a sacrificial animal, a basket, and a city. Yet the Bible's largest promises are attached to it. When God told Moses, "let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them"…

h8435.sum: Tôwlᵉdâh is the Hebrew word for the "generations" that come from a person or a starting point: the descendants, family lines, and unfolding history that follow from an origin. The NKJV translates it "genealogy," "genealogies," "generations," "history," "records," and once "birth." It gives Genesis its framework. Again and again the book pauses to say, "This is the genealogy of…" or "This is the history of…", and…

h8449.sum: The Hebrew word tôwr names the turtledove, a small, gentle, migratory bird of the dove family. Most of its biblical uses are found at the altar. In Leviticus, God allowed a poor Israelite who could not afford a lamb to bring "two turtledoves or two young pigeons" instead. Poverty did not shut anyone out of atonement, cleansing, or restoration. The bird appears even earlier, in Genesis 15, among the animals Abram…

h8454.sum: Tûwshîyâh is a Hebrew word for wisdom that works. The NKJV translates it as "sound wisdom," "success," "prudence," "plans," "judgment," and "guidance." The range of translations makes sense once we see the idea behind them. This word describes good sense and the ability to carry it through to a good result. It is wisdom with substance, the kind that holds up when life puts weight on it.

h8478.g: Because, because, below, beneath, instead, place, places, Under, under
h8478.sum: Tachath is a common Hebrew word of position. At its simplest it means "under," "beneath," or "below": the waters under the firmament, a traveler resting under a tree, enemies brought low under a king's feet. From that idea of standing in a spot it also comes to mean "in place of" or "instead of," the place one thing takes when another is removed or exchanged. A son reigns in his father's place, and a ram is offered…

h8485.sum: Tema was the ninth listed son of Ishmael. His name also became the name of the tribe descended from him and of their settlement, a well-watered oasis in northwestern Arabia on the caravan routes that ran between southern Arabia and the lands to the north. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It is sometimes linked to a root meaning "desert" or to the idea of "south," but neither derivation is established. Tema…

h8487.sum: Teman is first a man and then a land. He was the first listed son of Eliphaz and a grandson of Esau, and he became one of the chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 15). His name came to belong to an important region of Edom, so prominent that the prophets often used "Teman" to stand for the whole Edomite nation. The name means "south." It is related to the Hebrew word for "right hand," because a person facing the sunrise…

h8489.sum: "Temanite" names a person who comes from Teman, a leading region or town of Edom, the land settled by the descendants of Esau. The word describes origin, so its meaning is simply "one from Teman." The place name Teman is generally connected with the Hebrew word for "right hand," and from that with "south," because a person facing east to get his bearings has the south on his right. That derivation is widely held but…

h8490.sum: The Hebrew word tîymârâh means a column of smoke rising into the sky. It appears only twice in the Bible, and each time the NKJV translates it "pillars of smoke." Lexicons commonly connect it with the Hebrew word for a palm tree. If that derivation is right, it may suggest a plume that climbs straight up like a trunk and then spreads out at the top, though neither verse describes the smoke's shape. This word does…

h8494.sum: Tiras is the last of the seven sons of Japheth listed in the Table of Nations. He is a grandson of Noah, and he stands as the ancestor of a people who settled somewhere in the wider world after the Flood (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). The meaning of his name is uncertain. It is probably not a Hebrew word at all but a name drawn from a non-Semitic language of the distant north or west, and Scripture offers no…

h85.sum: Abraham is the patriarch whom God called out of a family that worshiped other gods. God made him the father of Israel and, through his Seed, the father of all who believe. He was born Abram, a name usually understood to mean "exalted father." When he was ninety-nine, God renamed him Abraham, and Scripture explains the new name itself: "for I have made you a father of many nations" (Genesis 17:5). The Hebrew sound of…

h8518.g: Hang, hang, hanged, hanging, hangs, hung
h8518.sum: The Hebrew verb talah means to hang or to suspend . Scripture uses it for ordinary things: shields hung on a tower, harps hung on willow branches, cups and pitchers hung on a peg. It is also used for something far darker, the public hanging of a human body. Where the Bible spells out the order of events, as in Deuteronomy and Joshua, the person had already been put to death, and the body was displayed so that the…

h8530.sum: The Hebrew word translated "armory" appears only once in the Bible, in the bridegroom's praise of his bride in Song of Solomon 4:4: "Your neck is like the tower of David, built for an armory, on which hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men." Scholars disagree about the word's exact origin, and this single verse does not settle its precise meaning. What the verse does make clear is the scene: a tall…

h8534.sum: The Hebrew word taltal describes hair that hangs in thick, flowing locks. The NKJV translates it "wavy." It appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 5:11, where the bride describes the man she loves: "His head is like the finest gold; His locks are wavy, And black as a raven." Because the word occurs only once, its exact shade of meaning is uncertain. One ancient reading connected it with the drooping…

h8535.sum: The Hebrew word tâm describes a person who is whole and complete. Applied to character, it means someone whose life holds together: not divided, not two-faced, consistently turned toward God. The NKJV usually renders it "blameless." The word does not mean sinless. It describes integrity, a life without hidden double-dealing, and Scripture pairs it with fearing God and turning from evil.

h8549.sum: The Hebrew word tâmîym describes something whole, sound and complete, with nothing missing or damaged. It most often describes the animals Israel brought to the LORD, which had to be "without blemish," such as the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:5) and the daily burnt offerings. The same word also describes people who walk with God with their whole heart. Noah was "perfect in his generations," and God told Abraham, "walk…

h8555.sum: Timna is a name from the family records of Edom in Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1. It most clearly belongs to a Horite woman, the sister of Lotan and daughter of Seir, the original people of the mountain country south of the Dead Sea. She became the concubine of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn son, and bore him Amalek. The same Hebrew name later appears among the "chiefs" of Edom, where the NKJV spells it "Timnah." The…

h8558.sum: The Hebrew word tâmâr means palm tree , the tall date palm that marked water and life across the dry lands of the Bible. Scripture uses it a dozen times. The palm appears at Elim, where Israel camped after the bitter water of Marah. Its branches were taken up at the Feast of Tabernacles, where God commanded His people to rejoice. It names Jericho, "the city of palm trees." In poetry it pictures the flourishing…

h8588.sum: The Hebrew word taʻănûwg names something delightful: a luxury, an exquisite pleasure, or something tenderly cherished. It is rare, appearing only five times, and those few uses cover a wide range of human life. A fool surrounded by luxury looks out of place (Proverbs 19:10). A king gathers "the delights of the sons of men" and finds them empty (Ecclesiastes 2:8). A husband rejoices over his bride "with your…

h8598.sum: The Hebrew word tappûwach names a fruit tree and its fruit, usually translated "apple" or "apple tree." It is a rare word, used only six times, and almost always in poetry. Each time, the tree or its fruit stands for something sweet, refreshing, or precious. In Proverbs 25:11 a well-timed word is "like apples of gold in settings of silver." In the Song of Solomon the bride compares her beloved to an apple tree…

h8646.sum: Terah is best known as the father of Abram (later Abraham), Nahor, and Haran. He was a descendant of Shem who lived in Ur of the Chaldeans, led his household out toward Canaan, stopped at Haran, and died there at two hundred and five years old (Genesis 11:24–32). The same Hebrew name also labels an unrelated place, a camp where Israel stopped during the wilderness years (Numbers 33:27–28). The meaning of the name is…

h8656.sum: In the Old Testament, Tirzah is the name of a woman and of a city. The woman belonged to the tribe of Manasseh and was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad. She and her sisters stood at the doorway of the tabernacle and asked for a share of the Promised Land because their father had died without sons. The city lay in the hill country of Manasseh. Joshua defeated its Canaanite king, and Tirzah later became the…

h8659.sum: Tarshish is best known in the Bible as a distant, wealthy seaport or region at the far edge of the ancient world, famous for its silver and metals and for the large ocean-going "ships of Tarshish" named after it. The same Hebrew name also belongs to three different men: a grandson of Japheth in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:4), a Benjamite (1 Chronicles 7:10), and a Persian prince at the court of Ahasuerus…

h8669.sum: This Hebrew word for "desire" describes a strong longing or urge that pulls one person toward another. It appears only three times in the Bible, and those three uses tell a story. In Genesis 3:16, after the Fall, God tells the woman, "Your desire shall be for your husband, And he shall rule over you." In Genesis 4:7, God warns Cain that sin crouches at his door: "its desire is for you, but you should rule over it."…

h87.sum: Abram is the son of Terah from Ur of the Chaldeans. God called him to leave his homeland and go to a land He would show him, and he became the man through whom God promised to bless "all the families of the earth" (Genesis 12:3). His name is widely understood to mean "exalted father," from the Hebrew words for "father" and "exalted." For most of his story that name sat uneasily on him, because he and Sarai had no…

h875.sum: The Hebrew word bᵉʼêr means a well: a shaft dug down through the earth until it reaches water hidden underground. In the dry lands of the Bible, a well meant life for people and flocks, a claim to land, and a place where people met. The same word can also describe a pit, from the asphalt pits of the Valley of Siddim to the "pit of destruction" in the Psalms. What a hole in the ground means depends on whether it…

h911.sum: Bedad was an Edomite, a descendant of Esau's people, and Scripture remembers him only as the father of Hadad, one of the early kings of Edom. His name appears twice, in parallel records: "Hadad the son of Bedad, who attacked Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his place" (Genesis 36:35; 1 Chronicles 1:46). The name is derived from a Hebrew root meaning "to be separated" or "to be alone," so it likely carries the…

h93.sum: The Hebrew word ʼĕgôwz means nut , and it is generally understood to mean the walnut tree and its fruit. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 6:11: "I went down to the garden of nuts." Because the word appears only once, everything we learn from it comes from that one verse and the love poetry around it. The verse describes someone going down into a cultivated grove in springtime to see whether the…

h935.g: Bring, bring, bringing, brings, brought, Came, came, certainly, Come, come, Comes, comes, coming, enter, entered, entering, entrance, Go, go, goes, going, gone, had, has, have, indeed, put, surely, take, took, went, you
h935.sum: The Hebrew verb bôwʼ means to come , to come in , or to enter . In a related form it means to bring , that is, to cause someone or something to come in. It is one of the most common verbs in the Old Testament. Scripture uses it for everyday movement such as entering a tent, arriving at a city, or bringing a meal. It also uses the same verb for some of the weightiest movements in the Bible: God bringing His people…

h936.sum: The Hebrew verb bûwz means to despise: to look at someone or something and decide it has no worth. It is an active judgment. In many of its uses it is a sinful verdict. Proverbs uses it for the fool who despises wisdom and instruction, the person who despises God's word, the neighbor, or an aging mother. The Bible treats this contempt as more than bad manners. It is a refusal of what God Himself values, and it leads…

h990.sum: The Hebrew word beṭen names the belly, the soft middle of the body. Scripture uses it for the stomach that hungers, the womb where a child grows, and, by extension, a person's inner being, the hidden depths that no one else can see. The NKJV most often renders it "womb." In the phrase "the fruit of your body," it also means children.
